subtopic: DAMAGE IN WESTERN ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government has been giving consideration to the question of assisting those who suffered loss by reason of the tornadoes, which caused considerable damage in western Ontario on May 21 and May 24, 1953.
The counties of Lambton, Middlesex, Oxford, Perth and Huron set up county relief committees to which donations were made by individuals and municipal corporations. The provincial government has assured a grant being one-half the amount which came into the hands of the county relief committees, from these two sources. Donations totalled $210,425 and the municipal grants $64,500, which means that the provincial grant would amount to $137,462. The Canadian disaster relief fund announced last week that it would contribute $100,000 to the relief funds and this is to announce that this government will contribute the sum of $137,462 for the benefit of those who suffered loss to dwellings and farm buildings, being a like amount to that contributed by the province of Ontario.
Details of the method of payment will be worked out with the Canadian disaster relief fund and the county committees.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday, in response to a question from the hon. member for Prince Albert concerning Igor Gouzenko, the Prime Minister stated that he was not aware that any further representations on this matter had been received from the United States Department of State for Mr. Gouzenko to be interviewed but that he would inquire of me whether that was the situation. I should now like to confirm that, up to the present, we have received no further representations from the United States to interview this man.
I believe that it would be useful if I took this opportunity to say a few words on this matter because yesterday the hon. member for Prince Albert asked if the government was now giving reconsideration to the original request for an interview. As hon. members may know, the government on October 29 received a request from the United States government transmitting a request from Mr. Robert Morris, counsel for the United States Senate internal security subcommittee, to interview Igor Gouzenko in this country. These requests arose out of a statement which Mr. Gouzenko was reported to have made to the reporter of the Chicago Tribune to the effect that he had some further information, and that he would be glad to appear before the United States Senate subcommittee. When this report appeared in the press the Royal Canadian Mounted Police immediately interviewed Mr. Gouzenko to ascertain whether he had such additional information since, if he did, this information should have been passed on to the Canadian authorities and that part of it, if any, of interest to the appropriate United States authorities would have been forwarded to them. The interview
80	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry was made by the R.C.M.P. before the request was received from the United States state department-that is, the request which I have just mentioned.
When interviewed, Mr. Gouzenko informed the R.C.M.P. that he had no further information to offer other than that which had already been reported by the royal commission some years ago. He further stated to the R.C.M.P. that he had been misquoted by the Chicago Tribune, and he denied that he had criticized the manner in which his evidence had been used. In the circumstances the Canadian government, Mr. Speaker, considered that the reasons for Mr. Morris' request to interview Mr. Gouzenko had disappeared, having been based on a misunderstanding of the position.
I might add, Mr. Speaker, that any information from Mr. Gouzenko which could have been of value to the United States authorities had originally been forwarded to them as soon as it became available. We have cooperated in the past and will, of course, in the future co-operate fully and in the proper manner with the United States government in these matters.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, November 16, consideration of the motion of Mr. A. H. Hollingworth for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Drew, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose yesterday evening I had just presented some facts in connection with the economic position of agriculture in this country and indicated there was a serious downward trend in the income of agriculture in the past two years. This trend, sir, is more noticeable, particularly in the livestock industry today, and I believe that no time
The Address-Mr. Zaplitny should be lost in instituting action to provide a more solid base and greater stabilization for the industry and the production of livestock. I would like therefore to put on record three recommendations, made by the prairie farm unions, of which I believe the government is already aware.
They are as follows:
(1)	The establishment of a national livestock marketing board, upon which the producers from each province will he adequately represented, to be charged with tile responsibility of setting and maintaining a fair and adequate floor price on livestock with fair price spreads for the different grades.
(2)	The adoption of a policy under which the board would establish a price for the products probably required for consumption in Canada, based on a proper and fair relationship to other goods and services within our Canadian economy, the balance to be disposed of in world, markets to the best advantage of the producer.
(3)	The provision for the necessary additional cold storage facilities in western Canada, made available to the livestock industry on much the same basis as government terminal elevators are made available for grain, as part of a national program of orderly marketing of much needed foodstuffs, in the interest of both producers and consumers.
A livestock marketing board is not a particularly new subject in the house. It has been urged upon the government repeatedly, particularly by the former member for Selkirk. However, at this time I think there is more reason for the existence of such a board than there ever was before. As I have pointed out, the sharp decline in returns on livestock is one of the reasons; and there is also the additional and quite important one in the fact that at the present time livestock producers, particularly the producers of beef, have no protection whatsoever in the grading or handling of their product. They do not have the protection given the grain producers through the board of grain commissioners, whereby a proper grading is guaranteed.
As the situation now stands, strange as it may sound it is quite possible to ship a choice steer and have it graded as an old cow; and in such event there is no one to whom the producer can complain. There is no authority at all for the protection of the producer in this matter of grading, and there is evidence to show that in that respect advantage is being taken of the producer.
There are some further recommendations I should like to place upon the record, based upon the study of the situation I have made. I believe that these would have the effect of stabilizing farm income and providing a better position in the future.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Does the hon. member say that there is no grading of livestock, that a steer could be graded as a cow? Has he had any

The Address-Mr. Zaplitny experience in the marketing of cattle through the union stockyards at Winnipeg? I refer to the stockyards at St. Boniface.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: No, I have not had personal experience in marketing livestock at the stockyards.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Then why do you make the charge? Why does the hon. member say that a steer can be graded as a cow?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Of course I was using a figure of speech.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: They would probably call it a canner.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I would hardly imagine that there would be persons who would not know a steer from a cow-although, if one might judge from what he hears at times in the house, he might come to that conclusion.
The situation is simply this, that there is no statutory protection, no legislation to provide for the protection of the producer, so far as the grading of his product is concerned; and I suggest that provision should be made. If the hon. member who asked the question does not think any such protection is required, then of course he is at liberty to say so, and I shall be glad to hear him.
I wish now to move on to another recommendation, and that is that a full investigation should be made into the prices of farm implements and farm fuels. The situation today is that while the income on farm products has been declining sharply, prices of farm implements and fuels have continued to rise. Only recently fuel prices took another upward jump. This places the producer in a squeeze where, eventually, if the trend continues, he will not be able to produce any longer, because his costs of production will catch up to his returns and reach a point where farming will no longer be economical.
However, in making such an investigation- and in what I am about to say I realize my proposal is not new, because it has been made before even in parliament-I would emphasize that I am not interested in a committee or commission or investigation set up for the purpose of creating the impression that something is being done about the problem. That has been done before. I have sat on committees, as I am sure have other members in the house, which spent weeks and months, during which time they did some very valuable research work. But their findings and recommendations are still gathering dust on the shelves of parliament. That is not the kind of investigation in which the farmers are interested. We do not ask for


a whitewashing job: we want an investigation which, if it discloses exploitation or profiteering, will bring forth prompt remedial action. If it is found that profiteering exists, then this parliament should have the courage to reimpose price controls immediately and, if necessary, provide subsidies in order to bring prices back into a proper alignment.
I believe the people of this country are tired and resentful of the fact that there have been numerous commissions and committees set up to investigate a subject; then, when they have done so, and have made certain findings and recommendations, nothing more has been heard about them. If we are going to have an investigation, let us have a genuine one, and let it be followed by appropriate action.
I would also recommend that, as one of the means of keeping the farm population in proper ratio to that of the nation, industry should be introduced to and extended in the prairie provinces. We now have in those provinces some manufacturing and processing; but the possibilities are much greater than can even be imagined at this stage. We have on the prairies many of the raw materials which would be required for the processing and manufacturing of many of those things for which there is a ready market right in those communities. To give an example, I would refer to the manufacturing and processing of vegetable oils, particularly linseed oil, which is so important in the paint industry; and I would also refer to the manufacture of glass, which requires a special type of sand. And, for the information of anyone who might be interested in this particular industry, I would announce that right in my own constituency we have one of the finest deposits of silica sand to be found anywhere in western Canada. We have also some of the finest deposits of pottery clay discovered anywhere in the west.
There are many other raw materials which make it possible to start industries and to provide steady employment, as well as to give economic balance to the economy of the west. At the moment we are too dependent upon production from the soil. There are times when the slack could be taken up, and seasonal employment provided for thousands of people who today have to go either to British Columbia in the west or to the eastern cities to find work in the winter months.
I would point out further that in Manitoba we have one of the best copper producing areas in the whole of Canada. Flin Flon, the copper capital of the west, is a centre which is growing by leaps and bounds. The production of copper has been increasing, and

has been brought to a greater degree of refinement. It would be quite feasible to establish manufacturing industries near the source of supply, and they should be as close as possible thereto.
Lastly, I should like to recommend, as a means of stimulating the proportion of rural population, loans to prospective young farmers, for the purpose of making it possible for them to begin farming. I am quite aware that we have the Canadian farm loan board, and that farm improvement loans are available. It has been the experience of those who have had anything to do with them that the persons who require the loans most are the ones least likely to be able to get them, because the loans are based upon a certain amount of collateral and security which quite often the young man who wishes to buy a farm 'or equip his farm simply cannot provide. It is, again, one of those things like bank loans. It is easy to borrow an umbrella when the sun is shining. Those who do not need the loans can go in and get them, but those who wish to start farming have no collateral, and perhaps no security to offer, and they find that they are simply left out in the cold.
I realize that if we went further and were more lenient in providing loans there would be an element of risk, but whatever little risk would be involved would be far outweighed by the advantage of keeping these young men who are interested in farming on the farms and giving them an opportunity to start on their own in developing the western prairie provinces to a greater extent.
Some people in Canada may be under the impression that there is no arable land left undeveloped on the prairies. I would recommend that they take a trip through the west some time, particularly through the northern portions of the three prairie provinces, and they will find out how wrong they are. There is still a great deal of desirable land to be put under cultivation. Thousands of young men are desirous of going into farming on their own but the prices of land and farm equipment have reached such a height that one must almost be wealthy to start farming, and of course the philosophy is, if you are already wealthy why start farming? A great deal more leniency should be shown. Perhaps an entirely new set-up should1 be established to provide loans for men who do not have any collateral, but who are good moral risks and can be set up on their own.
This does not exhaust the possibilities in connection with agriculture, sir, but I will not prolong this discussion at this time. Before concluding I would simply like to make
The Address-Mr. Stick one reference to a statement that was made here this afternoon by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris). In view of that statement, which is very interesting to me, as it is to hon. members near me, who are familiar with the flood losses that I discussed yesterday, I am wondering whether the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) would be prepared to make a similar statement in connection with the problems we have out there.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Before going into the subject matter that I wish to discuss today, may I, Mr. Speaker, convey to you my congratulations on your unanimous election to preside over the deliberations of this house. Those of us who sat in the house when you occupied the Speaker's chair during the last session know that your elevation is an honour well deserved, and I wish to convey to you, sir, my very sincere wishes.
I should like also to take this opportunity to convey to the mover (Mr. Hollingworth) and the seconder (Mr. Villeneuve) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne my congratulations on their splendid effort. Some of us know what an ordeal it is to stand up in this house for the first time and address this gathering. That they acquitted themselves as they did shows that they have a future before them in this house.
Much discussion and much criticism of the length of the debate on the speech from the throne have been expressed in the press and elsewhere. It is said that this debate takes up too much of the time of the house, and therefore costs the taxpayers of this country too much money. There are two sides to this question, as there are usually two sides to every question. It is one of the opportunities given to private members to address the house and to bring to the attention of the house, and therefore to the attention of the Canadian nation, local problems for which hon. members are directly responsible, and also problems which affect the whole of the nation.
It has been said on many occasions that we should adopt the practice of Westminster. I submit that Westminster is one parliament and this is another; that the problems they have to deal with in England are not at all similar to the problems we have to deal with in Canada. This is a vast land occupied by a population which is scattered over three or four thousand miles from coast to coast. Our problems are vast, and this gives an opportunity to private members to bring before the house and the Canadian people some of the difficulties with which they have to deal.

The Address-Mr. Stick And it is vitally necessary to have that opportunity if we are to have a rounded out picture of Canada as it is today. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I make no apology for talking about conditions in my own province and bringing to the attention of this house some of the problems which we have faced in the past and which we are facing today.
I refer now to the fishery problems in Newfoundland' and in the Atlantic provinces. For four hundred and fifty odd years Newfoundland has lived by its fisheries. It was the discovery of great quantities of fish along our shores which brought people to settle in Newfoundland and attracted fishermen from France, Portugal and other European countries. What was true four hundred and fifty years ago is true today. But conditions have changed. We now find that the old methods by which we caught, cured and marketed fish are no longer satisfactory, and if we persist in this method our fishermen will not receive adequate rewards from which they can get a decent living.
It is not a new problem with us in Newfoundland; it has been with us for many, many years. The time has come, Mr. Speaker, when a different policy must be instituted by this federal government and by our provincial government so that the situation which faces us today can be met and the difficulties overcome, and this industry restored to the rightful place it should have in the Canadian economy. Old methods must change. The fishing industry, like all industries, if it is to be successful, must keep pace with modern scientific methods, with modern methods of marketing. If the industry fails in that respect, then the tens of thousands of our fishermen and their families will be living at such a low level of subsistence that something drastic will have to be done about it.
For many centuries our traditional markets were in Europe, in Brazil and in the West Indies. Prior to the first world war those people could afford to pay a decent price for our product and our fishermen received decent wages for their catch and they were able to carry on. But two world wars have impoverished those people. They cannot now pay a price sufficiently high to give our people a decent living. When you realize that today our fishermen receive less than a cent a pound for their fish you will understand that this cheap food at such a price is not able to give them a decent standard of living. That is the condition.
There are signs that the authorities both here in Ottawa and at home are aware of the problem which faces us today. It is gratifying

to note that in the speech from the throne reference has been made to this problem. It is also gratifying to note that a serious effort is being made at least to grapple with this problem. As I said a few moments ago it is not a new problem. It certainly is not a new problem-it is an old problem which requires new and up-to-date methods of handling. Far too long have the fisheries of this country been neglected. We have perhaps heard overmuch about wheat in this house-and quite rightly. Members who come from the wheat-growing prairies bring this matter to the proper authorities of government and the whole house and we do not object at all. It is their duty. However, I think it is time for those of us who come from the fishing areas to bring to the attention of the house problems regarding fishing.
The Department of Fisheries was known in the past as the "Cinderella" department of government. That day has now gone. It is no longer the Cinderella department of government; it is a very important department of government and it is high time that everyone in this house realized it. The fishing industry, since Newfoundland came into union, is worth something like $200 million a year. Neither this nor any other parliament can afford to neglect that industry. Something must be done.
I speak about this matter today and express my views about the problem which faces us in order to see if we cannot bring it to the attention of the house so that we may have the sympathetic consideration of all members of the house on all sides, so that our people not only of Newfoundland but of all the Atlantic provinces may have the better way of life to which they are entitled.
A change has taken place in fishing. The trend is to get away from the salt codfish and get into the fresh fish market. That is as it should be. When you lose your traditional markets, as we have lost and are losing them, you come into a period of transition where you have to change from one system to another. That period is a period of trial not only for those in authority but for those who prosecute the primary industry.
We have a market here in North America representing 170 million odd people. They need this fish and we have to see that we give it to them in a palatable form so that they will appreciate good food when they get it and ask for more. Furthermore, the population of North America-including Canada and the United States-is increasing at about three millions per year. There you have a continuing and growing market. It is up to the government and the industry together to see that this market is supplied with this nourishing food which comes from the sea. There is

a challenge, in the minds of the industry, to this government, the provincial governments and the fishing industry. If this challenge is met in the right way, in a very few years fishing problems will be solved and you will have a well-cared-for and contented fishing population. If the problems are not solved you will have a discontented people, and Canada cannot afford to have discontented people.
Our people back home are very much concerned with the situation as it presents itself to us today-and they are rightly concerned. We who stand up here and speak for our province are also concerned. Their general welfare is our first concern. So, Mr. Speaker,
I have no hesitation in saying what I say today and in appealing for sympathetic consideration of this problem by this house. I want the people of my province, and not only the people of my province but the people of all provinces, to be able to earn a decent living. They are entitled to that. We do not want to be pampered, sir; neither do we want anything that is not our just right. So, when we ask that this government here play its part in conjunction with our provincial government and with the fishing industry we are asking for something within our rights-and we make no excuse for asking for it.
I am glad to note, since I came to Ottawa for this session of parliament, that serious efforts are now being made to tackle this problem and to explore possibilities of better marketing so that our people may reap from the industry the benefit to which they are entitled.
I do not want to herald the subject. I could tell you tales of heroism, and tales of tragedy through which our people have passed many years ago, but I will say this. Over the doors of the entrance to this parliament are the words:
The wholesome sea is at her gates . . .
Her gates both east and west
Whoever was responsible for those words carved in the stone certainly knew something about the sea. The whole meaning of those words is summed up in the word "wholesome". Everything that comes from the sea is wholesome. You go to the sea in summer for your health. When you want to restore tired nerves you go and imbibe the breezes which come from the sea and which invigorate your mind, your body and your soul. You reap the benefit of them and you come away refreshed.
What applies by the seaside applies equally well to what comes from the sea and out of the sea. The food which comes from the sea is nourishing food which the people of this country need for a well-balanced diet.
The Address-Mr. Stick So, the fishing industry of which I speak needs encouragement. It needs looking into, and the problems concerned with it need to be solved. In solving those problems we will help ourselves to a better way of life. Yes; "the wholesome sea is at her gates". It is a wholesome and a nourishing diet we get from the sea. It is up to the fishing industry with assistance from the government to give the Canadian people this nourishing diet. I hope that the plans which were announced will prove successful.
What we need is a new fishing policy at least for the Atlantic provinces. I have no criticism, or very little criticism, of the work of the fisheries department in the past, except perhaps to say that in the past the policy has been to do only what they had to do. If that is going to be the future policy of our fisheries department it will fail. What we need today is an enlightened, energetic, progressive policy, not afraid to take legitimate risks. If we believe in the future of this industry and if we set our minds to it we will solve the problems; but if we take the attitude that we can only do what we have to do, then we will not solve those problems and they will go on as they have done for the past few years.
As I said before, there are signs that at last the problems with regard to the fisheries are beginning to be seriously taken into account. Those of us who come from fishing constituencies will be watching the progress very closely; and we shall be taking a keener interest in it than we have perhaps taken in the past in order that we may play our part here as Canadians worthy of the trust that sent us here.
I have one more matter to bring to the attention of this house, Mr. Speaker, and it is with a great deal of regret that I mention the subject. On a number of occasions in this house I have stated my faith in this country and I have stated the reasons for our coming into union. I do not want ever again to be obliged to stand up in this house and to defend the union which took place a few short years ago between Canada and Newfoundland. But when I read articles such as this one which I shall quote in a moment- in a respectable paper published in Canada and one that is read from coast to coast- I must take exception. It is taken from Toronto Saturday Night of recent date under the heading "Ottawa Letter". It reads as follows. Just listen to this:
Predictions made at the time of Newfoundland's entry to confederation, that it would provide Canadian governments with as many headaches as it did British governments, are coming true. Some years after William of Orange ascended the throne of

The Address-Mr.. Stick Britain, the importunate demands of the Scottish people and their spokesman, the Duke of Hamilton, for financial and other kinds of help so exasperated him that one day he cried out, "I wish to God that Scotland were 1,000 miles away and had the Duke of Hamilton as its King". Unless Mr. Smallwood's ministry can set the island's economic house in order, one of these days Mr, St. Laurent will be saying, "I wish to God that Newfoundland were 1,000 miles away and that Mr. Smallwood or Mr. Pickersgill were its King".
That may be funny. It may be funny to some hon. members but it is certainly not funny to us. Mr. Smallwood does not need me to defend him. He is well able to take care of himself. Whatever thoughts we may have about his policy with regard to Newfoundland, let me say this: he is working day and night to improve the condition of our people.
The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) does not need me to defend him nor to defend his action when he brought about union. I want to put the record straight on this matter. In all my association with the Prime Minister, never once, by word or implication, has he expressed any regrets about our coming into union. I have travelled across this country from coast to coast and have met many thousands of Canadian people but I have not found anything of that nature.
We came into union honestly and sincerely. The terms of union were brought about by free democratic processes by free democratic peoples. Let me say here once and for all that we did not have to come here. We could have gone elsewhere if we had wanted to do so. We are not asking for anything that is not rightly our due as Canadian citizens. Furthermore, let me say that we are not second-class Canadian citizens either. When we read articles such as this one casting reflections on our people, it is time for people to stand up in this house and to refute such statements; and the only ones who can do it properly are those who come from Newfoundland. The gentleman who wrote that article is no great Canadian. I call him a petty Canadian and I hope he is here now listening to me.
Time and again I have stated that we want our rights under union. Furthermore, we are going to have them. We have no regrets in union. I hope this will be the last time I will have to rise and speak in this house as I am now doing. We want our rights and nothing more. As I say, we could have gone elsewhere but we did not do so because we wanted to keep our association within the commonwealth. But if articles like this one are continually being written, the result will be to create dissatisfaction among our people back home, and the effects may be bad.
CMr. Stick.]
I did not have the privilege of being born a Canadian. I therefore probably cannot feel for Canada as do other hon. members. But at least I am a loyal Canadian, and probably I am a great deal more loyal to Canada than are some who were privileged to be bom Canadians. I want to say now for the last time that this act of union was an act of faith on our part and on yours. As time goes on we hope that this act of faith will be cemented into acts of friendship whereby our two peoples can be as one, and whereby this country can be united as never before. Unless we have this unity, Canada cannot fulfil the high hopes which we have for her and the destiny which lies ahead.
Finally I want to say this. For many years and many centuries it was our proud boast that we were Britain's most ancient colony. I hope I may never live to see the day that I would regret helping to bring Newfoundland into union with Canada. However, I do hope that I shall live to see the day when we can change that proud boast, which we made for many years, and turn it into this sort of boast, namely, that we are Canada's newest and, I hope, most loyal province.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate you on your election as Speaker of the twenty-second parliament. I regard it as a well deserved honour. From your actions in the past, which have been indicative of your good judgment, your fairness and your understanding of this house, I am sure that in the days to come you will be regarded as one of the best Speakers we have ever had.
I should like to mention, sir, that in the four counties which comprise my riding, namely Hastings, Peterborough, Addington and Frontenac there is at the present time a great mineral development going on. For some time past many Canadian companies have had exploration crews searching for iron and uranium. Much work has been done and much more work is planned for the future. Many claims have been staked. Some of the properties will soon be in development. The most outstanding one is the Bethlehem Steel Corporation development at the village of Marmora,
In December last the premier of Ontario and officials from the mines department visited the property, and on that occasion it was stated that well over $30 million would have to be expended before this iron mine could be brought into production. This large deposit was located by an aeromagnetic survey, and the huge expenditure of money necessarily being made by the company to bring the property into production is just another example of the risk that must be

taken by private enterprise in any mineral development. No doubt there are many other deposits of a similar nature in the same district, which is just on the edge of the preCambrian shield, and I suggest to the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prud-ham) that further surveys be made in the area.
Yesterday the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) gave a short report in the house on restrictive trade practices. It is interesting to note in this morning's press a report of proceedings in Toronto yesterday in which eight rubber companies pleaded guilty to the charge that they had conspired to fix prices over a fifteen-year period. But what is more interesting are certain remarks made by crown counsel, Mr. T. N. Phelan, Q.C., reported as follows:
Mr. Phelan claimed that the accused had maintained "exact, complete and meticulous control over prices and distribution, destroying every vestige of competition." At the same time, he said, the rubber industry enjoyed a protective tariff of never less than 22 j per cent.
I suggest to the Minister of Justice that he would also do well to look into the question of the price of gasoline in Canada. The average motorist is unable to understand or comprehend why gasoline costs so much more in Canada than it does across the line. Is it due to excessive taxes or profits? The same thing applies to all electrical goods and motor cars. Take the average electric stove, which consists simply of several sheets of metal covered with a type of enamel and serviced by not more than six elements. Yet the retail price is around $300 or more. The same applies to other electrical devices, such as washing machines, refrigerators, toasters and so on.
If you buy a motor car today you are in the super-luxury class. Are the high prices charged Canadians due to excessive taxes imposed by the government or are the manufacturers obtaining huge profits? In a recent matter that came through my law office I was amazed to find that the great Chrysler Corporation of Canada, which manufactures Chrysler, De Soto, Dodge and Plymouth cars, makes no warranty in the sale of their cars. They advised me in connection with this matter as follows:
You will appreciate that the sale of the vehicle is by the dealer and not by the manufacturer. Accordingly the manufacturer does not make any warranty or representation with respect to the vehicle.
In fact, under the terms of the purchase, any such representation or warranty is specifically excluded. I think that will come as a great surprise to the public, certainly as a surprise to the purchasers of motor cars
The Address-Mr. G. S. White because surely every purchaser would naturally feel that when he purchases a new motor car he is not only relying on the skill of the manufacturer of the car but is also relying on the fact that there is an implied warranty that the car is fit and proper and will give the service for which it is intended. But the Chrysler corporation made it very plain to me that no such warranty exists, and if someone is unlucky or unfortunate enough to purchase one of their cars which is defective, a car that is a "lemon", he is simply out of luck as far as the corporation is concerned.
The matter with which I was dealing pertained to a new 1953 De Soto which was apparently one of the first few hundred cars manufactured of a new model. It appeared that everything that could possibly be wrong was wrong with the car. Here are just a few of the things. From the start the car burned oil and it still burns oil. The trunk was useless because it could not be locked. The lid of the trunk was always up. New locks were installed and it still would not work. The trunk accumulates dust, and puddles when it rains.
A new gas tank had to be installed but it is still defective. The windshield wipers would not work. New ones were put in but they still would not work. It is interesting to note that when the man received the car two of the hub caps were yellow and two were red. The corporation took four months to change them. The clock on the car did not work for eight months. The mechanism controlling the rear windows was put in upside down, and when it was adjusted the windows would not stay shut. The two rear doors were not adjusted properly and one had to squeeze into the car. The front seat would not remain locked in position. The windshield wipers would not wipe the glass clean, probably owing to a defect in the glass. The steering gear made most peculiar noises which were not very comforting to the driver. The fenders, hood and doors were not fitted properly, leaving cracks through which you could insert your finger. There were rattles in the car by the dozen which simply could not be eliminated. There was some difficulty with the fan which could not be properly adjusted, and a few other minor difficulties that did not appear to make much difference.
It would appear that an important company such as Chrysler, having turned out a lemon of a car like this, would at least replace it with a new car in proper shape. The purchaser paid a very fancy price and instead of having a new car from which he and his family could derive some pleasure he has a perpetual headache, and he got the very
88	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. G. S. White comforting information from this great corporation that it makes no warranty or representation of any kind as to the vehicle it manufactures. I hope that all purchasers of Chrysler products will take notice of the fact that this company makes no warranty of any kind and that the poor purchaser must look to the dealer for any remedy which he can get.
In the speech from the throne mention was made of veterans affairs but there was no indication that the government intends to increase the war veterans allowance. A press report relating to the brief submitted by the Legion to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the cabinet a few days ago contains this information:
The Legion recommended that the basic rate of war veterans allowance be increased to $60 from $50 a month for a single veteran and to $120 from $80 a month for married persons.
The Legion also urged that ceilings on total permissible income under war veterans allowance be increased to $1,200 per year for a single recipient and $2,000 a year for married persons. The ceilings now are around $850 and $1,200 respectively. The brief said many war veteran recipients are suffering very real hardship under present basic rates and restrictive ceilings on total permissible income.
The Legion's suggested housing plan would permit veterans to build their own homes on city lots as well as on small rural holdings as provided now under the Veterans Land Act.
A question was asked the minister a few days ago as to whether or not he intended to set up a committee on veterans affairs. At that time he said the matter was still under review. This matter of veterans allowances has been before the house on many occasions.
I do not think any hon. member is going to disagree with the brief submitted by the Legion in which they ask for a basic rate of $50 a month for single veterans and $120 a month for married veterans.
The Minister of Veterans Affairs was asked a question today about casual earnings and I sincerely hope that it is not the intention of the government to reduce in any way the small casual earnings that are now permitted to veterans.
The brief goes on to say that another major recommendation dealt with pensions. It proposes that in cases where pension applicants are found to have disabilities resulting from injuries or diseases not recorded on medical examination at enlistment such injuries or diseases should be presumed to have occurred or had their inception after enlistment. But the pension board, with their great knowledge, are often and practically always able to find that the disability was incurred prior to enlistment, that it was not aggravated by war service and therefore the veteran is not entitled to a pension. The
[Mr. White (Hastings-Frontenac) .1

medical doctors on the pension board make that finding despite the fact that the veteran may have been and probably was A-l on enlistment after a very thorough and complete examination with X-rays.
It seems to me that in far too many cases that clause in the act which stated that the veteran shall have the benefit of the doubt does not apply. I have said before in this house, and I say again, that it should never be necessary for any veteran to have to go to his reeve or to his member of parliament or to anybody else to get his pension or other claim properly adjusted. I regret to say, Mr. Speaker, that in far too many cases that have come to my attention little if anything is done until the veteran's case is brought to me and then in some cases he is roundly abused as to why he went to his member of parliament.
The people of Canada want the veteran to have everything to which he is entitled, and no veteran should have to fight the whole pension board and a host of medical men. Too often when the veteran is called in for an examination he is treated as a lead-swinger and bluntly told to go home, there is nothing wrong with him. But the record shows that the pension board has made many mistakes in the past, and they will continue to make many mistakes in the future. I find that the veteran resents in many cases the very casual manner in which he receives his medical examination. Little or no attention is paid to the reports that he will produce from his home physician.
The matter of small holdings under the V.L.A. is preventing many veterans from receiving the benefit of this act because of the restriction in 'the act as to the number of acres held, and owing to the increase in assessments the veteran finds that he is often penalized in heavy taxes for the extra land that he must have in order to qualify under the act. There are many other matters relating to veterans affairs which in my opinion would warrant the minister setting up a committee on veterans affairs, and I hope that he will announce the setting up of such a committee.
The hon. member for York Centre (Mr. Hollingworth) in moving the adoption of the address, and to speaking of the result of the election, used these unfortunate words, which appear on page 13 of Hansard for November 13, 1953:
. . . the results showed the good common sense and the political maturity of the Canadian people from coast to coast.
Well, despite what the hon. member said, I would say to the government that in my riding the people showed good common sense

and political maturity in rejecting the policies of this government. By their vote they have registered a strong protest against high taxation, the loss of markets, and the waste and extravagance of this government and their drift to socialism and1 paternalism. During the election the government made every effort under the sun to convince the voters of my riding that it deserved their votes. They even went so far as to have the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) speak in my riding, and I would like to take this opportunity of thanking the two ministers for their visit. I am only sorry they did not stay longer, because if they had I would have had several thousand more votes.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce, speaking at the village of Marmora, as reported in the Ontario Intelligencer of July 27, said:
Canada is not on the verge of losing her markets abroad. That flat statement was made here on Saturday by Et. Hon. C. D. Howe, Minister of Trade and Commerce and Minister of Defence Production.
It is rather unfortunate that when the minister was in the centre of a very fine agricultural district he did not go on to explain to the dairy producers, the cheese producers and all the other producers just where these markets are today. It would have been very interesting if he had explained to all these producers where they were going to sell their products. There seems to be an attitude on the part of many people that there is no need to compare the prices of farm products with those of other commodities. Certainly high prices exist in other commodities and also exist in some foods and manufactured goods and are the cause of hardship, but for some unknown reason the public expects dairy products to be sold at levels lower than those of other commodities.
We should remember that there are over
400,000	dairy farmers who, together with their families and all the people from whom they purchase, consume large quantities of manufactured products. We in Canada cannot afford to have the income of such a large group of people reduced so that their buying power will be impaired,
The present condition of the companies that manufacture agricultural implements is just an example of what happens when the buying power of the farming community is reduced.
Speaking in the debate last night, the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Mac-Dougall) mentioned the elimination of the means test with respect to pensions for the blind. I concur in those remarks. I think that all members greatly admire the work
The Address-Mr. G. S. White that has been done by various associations connected with the blind attempting to assist them in their re-establishment. But the blind pension is subject to the means test, which simply means that when a blind person reaches the age of seventy years and is entitled to the universal old age pension he will then lose part or all of his blind pension. The number of blind over seventy years who would need both pensions must necessarily be very small. I am sure those who need it would be most grateful if this means test could be removed. All members have received a brief and a letter in connection with the matter, summarizing it; and I sincerely hope the government will give earnest consideration to this request.
My leader has moved the following amendment:
We respectfully represent to Your Excellency that the welfare of Canada is dependent upon free competition; and that the prosperity and security of all Canadians will be advanced by government policies which will restore markets for primary products and generally promote a high volume of international trade.
I intend to support that amendment, for certainly the welfare of Canada is dependent upon free competition. In this Canada of ours, with its great wealth. of natural resources, there is every opportunity for youth and for all others who are willing to work. But under socialism or state paternalism it would mean that we would take away from our youth all hope, ambition and initiative. It would mean that we would take away from our youth those things they would hope to gain for themselves and their families through the skill of their hands or their brains. If we take those things away from youth, then we will destroy for all time the very essence of those things which exist within each one of us, and which go to make a nation strong and great.

speechtext:
Mr. Deputy Speaker, the new Speaker has been congratulated by the hon. member who has just taken his seat, and I second his words. Now I congratulate you, sir, as his deputy. I am sure the house will be well directed both by Mr. Speaker and by Mr. Deputy Speaker, that they will be fair and just to all sides, and that they will be firm with those who attempt to break the rules.
I am happy to be here representing the constituency of Fort William, which is perhaps the cleanest and most progressive in Canada. I would not say that it showed outstanding common sense and prudence in sending me back; but they did so with the aid of two members of the official opposition who came to Fort William, both of whom
90	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Mclvor practically told my constituents that I would be back in the House of Commons. They are both members of our outstanding baseball team, and perhaps they said that because they felt they were likely to lose their places on the team. Anyone could see what that means. However, I can assure them that if I have anything to do with the baseball team representing the House 'of Commons no man who plays good baseball will ever lose his place, no matter what his political views may be-indeed, he might even be a Liberal.
I am happy indeed to have the honour of having as my deskmate a winner of the Victoria Cross. I am happy, too, to know that we have winners of that great honour on each side of the house, thus creating a splendid balance and showing that we are men of courage. Perhaps I might say that I feel somewhat easier, because I know that if I make mistakes my Victoria Cross colleague will guide me.
May I congratulate the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and all the members of his cabinet upon having been elected without making a single promise. Surely that is an outstanding achievement. I congratulate, too, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) upon his election, particularly in a constituency so outstandingly Liberal. I admire him in many ways, and it gives me great pleasure to look across the floor and see him happy in his heavy task.
I congratulate his chief assistant, and pay my tribute to him as one of those men who had something to do with helping to settle the pulp and paper industry strike, which seriously affected the lakehead. I welcome the new members, and I would say to them that those of us who come to this House of Commons, according to the estimate of a former lady member, compare favourably with any other group of men in Canada, not excepting the clergy. Therefore if any man comes to the house a bit unbalanced in his head, I suggest he should go back and take a back seat; otherwise he is likely to be told by someone in his own party to get out, and to get on the water wagon, and to conduct himself honestly as a good representative of his constituency.
The House of Commons, however, will never again be the same to me because of the loss of the former member for Peel.
I did not speak the other day; I felt the occasion was a tender one. But at this time I would say that on many occasions Gordon Graydon visited my room. We belonged to the same branch of the church and held some views in common. He was an outstanding


friend and, in practice, a happy Christian. I pay this tribute to him as one of Canada's greatest men who have crossed the river Jordan to join the others who have gone before. And I should like to add this, that if his good wife, so gifted and of fine character, should accept the nomination in that constituency, I would be greatly disappointed if a Liberal were nominated to oppose her. I hope we will have enough sense not to do it.
I welcome, too, the page boys, all but three of whom are new. Let me say to hon. members that these boys do a good job; do not give them any more to do than is necessary-and do not forget that they enjoy eats and drinks at the right time.
I congratulate the house, too, upon the return to parliament of every member of our baseball team. Surely this is a fine tribute to those who upheld the honour of the House of Commons. I would remind members of the press gallery that they will have to take care of their minds and bodies, and get down to practice earlier in the season, because again this year they are going to have a job on their hands.
As I turn to the speech from the throne I find three things which command particularly my appreciation. The first of these is the reference to trade. I know of course that any department headed by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) will do things for the benefit of Canada, no matter who may think to the contrary. As we listened the other day to the great President of the United States, saw his square face and his honest look, and heard his references to trade and other matters, I am sure we were inspired, even to the nerves in our diaphragms. Then when he lifted his eyes from his manuscript and dealt with the winning of the war, and concluded by saying that what we need on this great continent is faith in God and love for our fellow men, I was convinced indeed that the United States has a great president. I know that it will be taken care of. Nothing will be missed. If the opposition, like ourselves, have any suggestions to make, I am sure they will make them freely.
There is another thing in the speech from the throne that I appreciate very much, because we have been after it for a long while. The hon. member who just took his seat and many other hon. members supported the resolution that we have discussed many times. The handicapped people should have a pension. I said last year that I would not support any social legislation of any kind until those who cannot earn a dollar, and

must be completely attended to, have a pension. I thank the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) and the government for their Christian common sense and for bringing in this much-needed legislation.
I have a resolution on the order paper which will not be needed now.
Another thing that we at the lakehead appreciate very much is the reference to the gas pipe line. We think that we should have an all-Canadian pipe line. Since the announcement has been made in the speech from the throne it is likely that we shall have an all-Canadian pipe line. If I were allowed I would suggest a name for that pipe line. I would leave out the words "Right Honourable" and I would call it the "Louis" pipe line. That would be a good name for it. But I must not forget, Mr. Speaker, that this government has not all the say; the board of transport commissioners has not all the say; the people who are putting up the money, which is usually borrowed money, will have a good deal to say on whether the pipe line goes through or not. They must see a way of making a return for those who invest their money in it.
I should like to say a word or two about Fort William. Things have been happening up there, as you would expect. Few cities in Canada have grown more than we have during the last five years. Again I would congratulate the government on the aid they have given the McKellar hospital in opening a new wing which was badly needed.
Another thing we have at the lakehead- and I might speak for half an hour on it- is this. In the spring we are going to have a cobalt bomb to aid in the cure of cancer. This will be at Port Arthur. Then we have the Institute for the Blind in Port Arthur and Fort William. We have built a new home for the blind and it will soon be ready for work.
Then, we have a male choir at Fort William which stands high not only in Canada but in the United States. They went to the south and they covered themselves with glory and honour and were a credit to Canada. This year they are putting on an associated program with choirs from the northwestern states and Canada, in June, and I have had a partial promise that the rest of Canada will hear this program over the radio, and I hope it will materialize.
We have a rugger football team at Fort William that won out in the Canadian west. It is an intermediate team, but it is amateur. It is the only senior amateur rugger team in Canada that I know of. They have won
The Address-Mr. Mclvor out in the west and they will be coming down here to clean up in the east as well.
To those who have money to invest may I say that I have no apology to make when I assert that there is no other place in Canada that gives better promise than Fort William or Port Arthur. We have cheap power; we have transportation by land and water; we have fine paved highways, the Scott highway and the trans-Canada highway. As far as transportation is concerned no city is better situated than Fort William. As I said last year, we have the finest water supply system in Canada. It consists of a big lake 800 feet up mount McKay. We do not need any pressure to send that water all over the city. All they had to do was to build the viaduct down from the lake. The only thing is, they have to control it. There is no extra charge for quantity used. The more you use the better the water will be. You can start your hose running in the summertime and let it run all night and it will not do any harm to the city water supply; it helps it.
As I said last year, we have perhaps the best care for children, boys and girls and young people in Fort William that is to be found in any city in Canada. We have industrial playgrounds. We have paid workers during June and July, helped by our high school students. But those are well supervised. In the winter we have rinks. The rinks are all built now. We have twenty-four rinks, one rink for skating, and alongside it another rink for hockey, and they are well used. Our city council, backed up by the citizens generally, believe that if you keep a boy or girl busy with their hands and feet the police will have nothing to do. I pay my tribute to one big policeman who last year had charge of three hockey teams and this summer two baseball teams. That shows the relationship between the police of Fort William and our boys and girls.
Then, too, we have churches in Fort William that are on the job, Protestant, Roman Catholic and Jewish. They are on the job not with the object of making money and erecting buildings, but with the one outstanding idea of building up human beings and helping boys and girls to become true Christian Canadians.
We need some things, and I take this opportunity of saying that we need some things in Fort William, because of the coming of the great waterways which we hope will not be delayed very long. We need a new bridge across the Kaministikwia river. That is our first outstanding request. Because of the number of buildings that have to be rented, which cost the government a great deal, we are asking for a new federal building. Because
92	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Mclvor of the great attractions of our country, a citizen out west came into our city and wanted to be given the opportunity of spending $100,000 on a motel in front of mount McKay. We think that is one of the greatest attractions in Canada today. It has outstanding scenery, and opportunities for skiing, with one of the greatest ski jumps in Canada. We think that mount McKay should be a national park.
Then, we have tried to have television. I hope that will come. I hope the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation will give some attention to CKPR Fort William and CFPA Port Arthur so that they may combine to build a television station out there. I hope that will come about.
I have some suggestions to give to the government on behalf of all of Canada. As hon. members who have preceded me have said, I am thoroughly convinced that the outstanding need today is pensions for the blind without a means test. I think it will come, but we have to stick to it and prove that it is necessary and in the best interests of Canada.
I have three things to suggest to help the veterans. Prisoners at Hong Kong receive a pension. I think that prisoners of war in all other countries should have the same pension. It will be observed that the government has already taken steps to bring that about.
I know a young man, an outstanding young hockey player, a real rugged one, a fine athlete, who was shot down in Germany. His leg was broken and he did not have an easy time. One should consider the treatment received by that young man and I think he should have a pension, as would be the case for a prisoner who was confined in Hong Kong.
Mention has been made of the necessity of increasing pensions for our veterans. A single man unable to earn money should receive $60 a month and a married man should receive $120. These men gave their very best and risked everything while others stayed at home. The best that we can do for them is none too good.
Another suggestion with regard to veterans would be to assist those who served in the trenches. I know a man who ate four Christmas dinners in the trenches. He experienced wet feet, wet clothes and wet sleeping ground. That will take ten years from his life and I am therefore going to suggest to the veterans affairs committee or to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) that a veteran should receive his old age pension without a means test at age 60.
My last suggestion to the government may seem foolish to some but I will make it just


the same. In Canada today we have an abundance of wheat-we have wheat everywhere. It reminds me of the days of the depression when we tried to get bread for boys and girls, men and women, while our elevators were full. Why could it not have been distributed? Why could not a way have been found to buy that wheat and make it into bread to feed the hungry? I think that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), with the grey matter they possess, could put across this proposal. I suggest that $100 million be taken from war expenditures for the purchase of wheat. We should send the wheat to countries which have need of it. I think that step is absolutely necessary.
Mr. Speaker, ours is a Christian country. This house is opened in a Christian way and if we conclude prayers by saying "Our Father", we should be brothers the world over. There is nothing new about this suggestion. The Christian program is to feed the hungry, to clothe the naked, and to aid the sick. If our Christianity is real, let us put this thing across. I am sure it would be the finest cure for war and the finest stimulant for peace.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) closed on the note on which he did close. I wonder if he would back the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) if the minister were to adopt social credit technique in order to get the hundred million dollars' worth of wheat put into the hands of starving peoples. If he would, that would be a great honour to him, for the only device I know of which could be consistently used to accomplish that righteous objective would be social credit proposals.
I wish to congratulate the Speaker on his elevation to the high position that he now holds, and to express my confidence that he will discharge his responsibility in a way highly commendable and beneficial to all concerned. I would also like to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne on the work they have done.
My purpose today is to talk about wheat, the very thing the hon. member for Fort William was referring to. On behalf of the federal constituency of Lethbridge, which I have the honour to represent, I rise to speak regarding the wheat situation as it affects us in western Canada. Today I ask for five main measures to be adopted by the government:

1.	That money be advanced to farmers at interest not greater than 2 per cent for the construction of wheat storage facilities on the farms, storage facilities that will be adequate over a long period of years.
2.	That an early initial payment of not less than 75 cents per bushel be made to the farmer on each bushel of wheat adequately and of necessity stored on his farm.
3.	That on each bushel of wheat adequately and of necessity stored on his farm the farmer be paid storage comparable with the storage paid on each bushel of wheat stored in an elevator.
4.	That where it might appear advantageous, Canadian dollars be advanced to appropriate potential customers abroad with which they might buy Canadian wheat.
5.	That an appropriately similar measure be adopted in respect of any coarse grain or grains in respect of which there may be found to be a surplus threatening the wellbeing of Canadian farmers.
In making these requests I am expressing the desires of a large percentage of the people in my constituency, in fact of practically all people who have taken the trouble to think out this problem realistically.
May I read from an article appearing on page 5 of the Lethbridge Herald, of November 6, 1953, entitled "William Todd Heads Macleod Constituency". The constituency organization which was meeting on that occasion was the Social Credit provincial annual convention. Here is the resolution which they adopted:
The following resolution was passed by the convention and is being forwarded to the Alberta Social Credit League at Edmonton for presentation at the convention:
"Be it resolved that this body of Alberta Social Credit delegates in annual convention assembled does hereby request and urge that the dominion government of Canada, as soon as possible, take measures
(1)	to make available to wheat growers, at a rate not exceeding 2 per cent, funds with which to build granaries, adequate for permanent storage on the farms, of all wheat, for which, at any given time, the wheat board has insufficient storage capacity;
(2)	to make to growers an initial payment of not less than 75 cents per bushel on all wheat adequately and of necessity stored upon farms;
(3)	to pay the farmer on all wheat adequately and of necessity stored upon his farm, storage comparable with that paid on wheat stored in elevators;
(4)	to advance Canadian dollars to commonwealth nations or to other prospective purchasing nations which, because of the wide and increasing variety and extent of Canadian production, find themselves unable to sell Canada sufficient of their goods and services to obtain, through mutually beneficial trade, Canadian dollars with which to buy Canadian surplus wheat.
The Address-Mr. Blackmore
Be it further resolved:
That we urge that the dominion government adopt appropriately similar measures in dealing with other grain or grains in respect of which there may be found to be a surplus threatening the well-being of Canadian grain growers. And be it further resolved that we urge the Canadian government to obtain the money with which to make such provisions respecting our wheat, not through borrowing or taxing, but through the appropriate use of Canada's credit somewhat as Canada's finance minister did in 1917, creating $50,000,000 with which he provided Britain with the means of buying from Canada $50,000,000 worth of Canadian goods for helping to win world war I as stated in the report of the royal commission on banking and currency for Canada published 1933.
May I commend that last paragraph to the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) and to every other person, in the house and in the country who really desires to find a solution for the problem of the surplus production which is accumulating in Canada and in the United States.
On page 5 of the Lethbridge Herald of November 11, 1953, is a report from the Cardston provincial Social Credit constituency association. In this report appears substantially the same resolution as that which I have already read. This indicates that I have behind me from my own constituency considerable support for the suggestions which I have placed before the house today.
There may be those who will say that Canada cannot afford to pay the money which such a set of proposals would cost to implement. May I suggest that Canada cannot afford not to provide the money; even if she has to collect the money by taxation, Canada cannot afford not to spend the money to implement the proposals which I have made. If we do not store our grain on farms and if we do not pay our farmers the full price for the grain so stored, then we are going to face alternatives neither of which, I am sure, any hon. member of this house would willingly contemplate.
The first thing to be borne in mind in connection with this whole matter as to whether Canada can afford the money is this. Wheat is a food unsurpassed in the over-all essentials of nutritive value. Wheat, properly stored and supervised, is almost imperishable. Wheat is easy to store and care for. The wheat with which God has blessed us in such abundance recently is hard wheat, the finest wheat in the world. There is no discoverable limit to the prospective need and potential demand for our wheat. I think there is no doubt about that statement.
We have the gravest possible need for food. Those who say they know tell us that we have an annual increase in the world's population of upwards of 25 million people. They tell us that our population today is
94	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Blackmore far greater than our food production is capable of taking care of. Those are solemn facts. No member of this house will question them for one minute. I ask any hon. member of this house this question. Do you want too many men and women in this world to get hungry? Hungry men are like hungry animals; they are mighty dangerous creatures to tamper with. That is considering the matter on the most materialistic basis, without considering Christianity at all, and just as a matter of pure national defence. We get up here and prattle along in this house, a good many of us, talking about how we want to defend ourselves against communism. God has given us the very means right here in this country with which we can take measures designed to prevent people like, say, the British Guiana people or the Mau Mau of Africa from going communist; yet we do absolutely nothing about it. How can we consider ourselves to be intelligent when we do things of that sort?
Look across the line. I am not wishing to criticize the administration down there, but every hon. member has read with considerable dismay, I am sure, of the proposed drastic reduction in production in that nation next year in respect of most essential commodities.
I do not wish to speak harshly, but I just wonder how such a measure as that can be classed as anything but international crime, with 1,400 million people going to bed hungry every night, with probably three million of them starving to death every year. With the greatest single need confronting us being that of food, then the nation which above all nations is qualified to produce food restricts the production of it. And that proposal will be right before us here in Canada very soon unless we discover and apply some means of taking care of our abundant production so as to keep it off the domestic market when we want to keep it off, and so as to be able to avoid selling it abroad when we want to do that.
If anyone in the house has a more logical or a more dependable set of proposals than the ones I have advanced, I invite him to rise in his place and tell the house those proposals and show how they will work better than the ones I have suggested. As I said, there is no discoverable limit to the demand for Canadian wheat in the world if we can only learn how to put dollars in the hands of the needy people in order to enable them to buy our wheat. They cannot get dollars from us by the ordinary trading methods because we do not want their goods, even if they have the goods-which many of them have not- to trade with us for Canadian dollars. We rightly refuse to accept their goods because
[Mr. Blackmore.1

they compete with the production of our own industries. If there is anyone who can gainsay that, I ask him to make himself vocal. This indicates that we are faced with a genuine difficulty, and one that just cannot be soothed away by unctuous phrases and beautiful words.
I have said that wheat is probably the greatest single item of real wealth in the world. A bushel of wheat will feed a certain number of human beings just as well in one generation as it will in another. Its value is perpetual regardless of the dollars and cents value which may or may not be attached to it from one generation to another. I say that the most reliable form of wealth any person or nation can hold is a bushel of wheat. Other grains also are real wealth of the highest intrinsic value. I am sure everyone will agree with me in that respect. I refer to oats, barley, rye and flaxseed. Can you think of anything that you would rather have in your storehouse in case of famine, insurrection within your country, or attack from abroad which disrupted your whole social organization? Can you think of anything you would rather have in your storehouse than a good quantity of any one of those grains? They will keep life extant for a long time. Blessed be any country having [DOT]on hand an ample supply of any one of those grains. Many times blessed will be a people having in safe storage a bountiful reserve of -each of these grains. Such a people will have an inestimable advantage in case of crop failure, internal trouble, military attack. Such a people will be able to aid afflicted ones abroad in case of need.
The measures I ask for would ensure and stabilize in Canada just such a reserve. When the Lord is blessing us with great crops, now is our chance to do just that. The measures I ask for would ensure and stabilize markets for our farming areas and therefore for our manufacturers. I think no hon. member will seriously disagree with that. Our farmers might not be able to buy all the products of our manufacturers, but they would go a long way if they were provided with adequate purchasing power. These measures would go far toward cushioning Canada's economy against mishaps of international trade, depressions and the like. They would help to make physically possible in our economy what is financially possible, or financially possible what is physically possible.
It is physically possible for us to produce enough of every kind of grain to lay up a store that would last us for a generation. One thing we hesitate about is where we will get

the money. If a proposal is physically possible, then a realistic financial system will make it financially possible; and if it will not do that then the system is faulty and ought to be changed.
May I now consider in some detail the five requests I listed at the beginning of my talk. The first is loans at 2 per cent for storage construction. When a farmer is put under conditions where he cannot market his grain, why in the world should he not be assisted to the extent of letting him have loans at 2 per cent? In my province of Alberta the provincial government is lending scores of millions of dollars to towns and cities all over the province at 2 per cent with which they can build water works, set up electric light systems and do several other things, all self-liquidating projects. If Alberta can lend money at 2 per cent, then something must be radically wrong with the federal government if it cannot do likewise. To advance loans for the establishment of granaries that would preserve our grain in case of emergency for generations is certainly a self-liquidating project if anything is.
Second, I request an initial payment of not less than 75 cents per bushel. Notice that I said "not less". I do not believe 75 cents is enough. I think nothing short of $1 will be adequate to enable the farmers to clear off the expenses which have been incurred through costs of production and straighten themselves out for the next year of production so they do not have to be hampered, curtailed and restrained at every turn.
My third point is the payment of storage on farm-stored wheat. The ultimate result of that measure would be this: If a farmer sold wheat in a given bin, say a bushel of it, to the dominion government and the dominion government paid him the cost of the wheat in full so that the dominion government owned the wheat and then the dominion government went on paying him storage, such as is now paid1 the great elevators, the time would come, if the channels of trade were not cleared, when the farmer would own that wheat again as a result of his storage. He then would have on his farm a fine supply of wheat. I do not think there is a farmer anywhere living close to the grass roots who does not realize how valuable it is to have on his farm a good granary full of each and every kind of grain. That has been recognized ever since the farmer began to farm.
Why should the farmer not own the wheat? If the government has paid for a bushel of wheat and then through storage has sold it back to the farmer, then the farmer would justly own it. There would have to be an
The Address-Mr. Blackmore understanding, of course, whereby the farmer would not liberate the wheat again into the markets without the express consent and co-operation of the federal government. That would enable such a measure to be used without disrupting the internal price structure.

speechtext: Why grow any more crops? Just start that circle and keep it going.
