speechtext:
Surely anybody with half the intelligence of my hon. friend ought to be able to know that two bushels of grain on your farm are worth more than one. That should be easy to see. I am really surprised at my hon. friend. He has got out of practice since he was in the house the last time. The measure I am proposing, as I have already indicated, would put the country in a position to control the price of grain within the country, because all that is necessary if the price of grain begins to rise too high is to liberate a portion of the grain into the market, as the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has demonstrated in respect of butter time and time again-and all credit to him. If it is desired that the price should rise, then the grain can be neutralized so that it will not go on the market and affect the price.
It may be said that is impractical. I am not convinced that it is not practical. If we people who live in an age when we have jet planes and scores of other well-nigh miraculous things cannot discover the financial means whereby to make what is physically possible financially possible it is surely a terrible reflection on us.
The fourth proposal is that the dominion government be prepared to make advances abroad to enable outside peoples to buy our genuine surpluses, the surpluses that we do not feel we want to store on our farms-this will relieve my hon. friend-or surpluses that we believe we really should make accessible to the needy people of the world. These would be genuine surpluses over and above our own local needs either today or next week. To sell these abroad we would make advances of money to prospective purchasers such as India, Japan, Siam, Malaya and any others who are unable to buy enough of our grain, and thus allow them to buy our grain.
Somehow or other many people become greatly exercised when the meaning of this proposal becomes fixed in their minds. I talked with a man on the train on the way down who almost went into a paroxysm when it dawned on him that I was proposing to give grain away, an inconceivable thing to him. I said, "Brother, you do not hesitate a minute to give billions of dollars away in

The Address-Mr. Blackmore airplanes, bombs, tanks, bullets, and human lives. You do not hesitate a minute when a war is on, but when I propose, in order to avoid war, that you give some grain away by an indirect route that is not going to cost you anything financially, you balk at it. How do you make sense out of that?" He has not made sense out of it yet. He has not told me. That is a bald fact.
That is the way people from other planets must look at what we do here, if they are much more intelligent or advanced than we are, as we suppose they are. Some people say such a thing never was done. Well, read the report on the United States economy called "The United States in the World Economy" prepared under the chairmanship of Wayne C. Taylor, and submitted in 1943 to the government of the United States. Read it and see what happened between the United States and the rest of the world between 1918 and 1928. You will read that the United States loaned billions of dollars to nations all over the earth which those nations used to buy United States goods and it kept the United States prosperous, kept their people employed. Only when they ceased to lend that money did depression come, and that depression began to come in the very year they ceased to loan that money. When they loaned it they expected to get it back. They found out they could not get it back and they could not even get the interest, because when the nations who received the money undertook to repay in their own goods the United States shut out those goods because they would compete with their own products.
Read the report. It will be good for all the folks who do not agree with us when we say that a richly endowed nation can without financial cost give goods away. Now, the farmer in the United States, in the case of wheat; did he give his wheat away when those loans were made abroad to buy wheat? Not at all. He got his pay. Everybody in the nation got paid for everything he did. But the nation as a whole loaned money abroad to buy the goods and give him the pay. Now, much the same kind of thing happened in Canada in 1917, a thing many people will be surprised to learn. Take the report of the royal commission on banking and currency in Canada, published in 1933. Turn to page 22, paragraph 47; I am going to read from it to you. It would be good for all to start in and read the whole report right through. I think it would help solve the problem in the mind of the hon. member for Fort William, and I hope he will read it. By the way, I would like to congratulate a man of his age for 
standing up here and giving as good a speech as he did today. I hope some of his friends tell him.
I read from paragraph 47, page 22:
In the war session of August, 1914 . . .
Before we had a Bank of Canada.
. . . parliament raised the partially covered issue to $50 million. Subsequently an issue of $16 million was made . . .
Which means the minister of finance printed subsequently an issue of $16 million.
.	.	. against a deposit of railway securities
guaranteed by the dominion government, as well as an uncovered issue of $10 million for governmental purposes.
That means in effect that the minister of finance printed at that time $26 million, printed it much as the Bank of Canada prints bills now, only the Bank of Canada lends them. He spent them. He printed $26 million and with them helped pay for the war. Now, listen to the second point:
In 1917 an emergency issue of $50 million of dominion notes was made to finance war purchases in Canada by the British government.
I suggest to those people who went prattling around the country jabbering about funny money that before they make themselves nonsensical they read this report and learn something about what Canada did before we were afflicted with the Bank of Canada.
So I suggest that just as we made advances to Britain in world war I we could lend money abroad to needy peoples much as the United States did between 1918 and 1928. That money could be spent in Canada to buy our goods. Everybody would get paid for his goods and services. Some people say that would cause inflation. How would it cause inflation any more than if we sold goods abroad, say to France, and received solid gold in return and then we paid the money out to the farmer? It could not cause inflation. That is the essence of the fourth proposal.
Now, the fifth proposal is that we apply to other grains the principles we have thus far laid down with respect to wheat. Of course you could not be expected to pay 75 cents a bushel for this oats, barley, rye and flax, but whatever amount would be appropriate in relation to the given rate paid for wheat. And where necessary it could be stored away, or where necessary sold abroad, by the same device if we could not trade it abroad in mutually beneficial trade.
I have already told you where to get the money, and let no one scoff at this. In another speech which I hope to give before too

long I intend to trace the financial history of Canada from 1868 down to 1934 and show that every single dollar Canada used during those years was printed by the minister of finance between those years 1868 and 1934, every dollar except what the banks created. Then silly people prattle about funny money! And a good deal of the money after he printed it was spent into circulation rather than loaned into circulation.
There are some who will argue that the farmers do not need financial assistance to a greater extent than they are now getting. That is a common argument being made today. That is the argument implied by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) today. I do not know how in the world it is that the ministers have managed to seclude themselves, to isolate themselves in such an ivory tower that they have not heard about some of the things that have come to my attention. May I refer, for example, to the Manitoba Co-operator dated September 3, 1953. I am going to read rapidly what is written there:
Federation Seeks Federal Financial Aid for Farmers
The importance of immediately announcing and implementing a federal government plan to provide short term loans or other means of aid to farmers to meet current operating expenses during the congested marketing period, was urged, August 31, by J. T. McLean, executive secretary of the Manitoba federation of agriculture and co-operation, in a letter to Rt. Hon. C. D. Howe, Minister of Trade and Commerce.
He said that the initial cash receipts this fall will be probably in the neighbourhood of $400 per farm. In view of present high and rigid operating costs and other fall commitments characteristic of the farm, the present financial difficulties many farmers are now experiencing can be appreciated, he added.
Apparently the ministers of the government cannot appreciate these things. I would like to see them out on the farm for five, six or seven years; they would appreciate a lot of these things then, I could tell you.
Now, Manitoba has a good Liberal government. There are sensible people in Manitoba. They do not advocate extreme things like what I am advocating, yet they realize there is trouble there. Here is a statement from Alberta. It comes from a newspaper which has never been accused of being a Social Credit newspaper. It is an editorial dated September 26, 1953, in the Calgary Albertan:
The town of Vulcan, about 60 miles southeast of Calgary, is well known for its "elevator row". Eight grain companies have elevators and annexes there with a total capacity of 1,468,000 bushels, and two more elevators are being built which will raise the figure to 1,588,000. That's enough capacity to supply each person in Canada with about five loaves of bread.
Yet it isn't enough, at least not in this season of abundant production. The congestion is as serious at Vulcan as in most other places.
97
The Address-Mr. Blackmore
Listen to those words.
That total space of about a million and a half bushels is now completely filled, but with old crop. It will stay filled until there's room in the terminals at Vancouver to hold some of the grain. In fact about a quarter of that space is filled with low-grade 1951 crop, according to the Vulcan Advocate, and there's no telling when that will be moved. Apparently there's no market for it, not with so much good wheat available.
The initial delivery quota this fall is only three bushels per cultivated acre, but the Vulcan elevators won't be able to take even a bushel for a long while yet.
About 180,000 acres of farm land is tributary to the Vulcan grain elevators, and about half that is in wheat, another 13,000 acres in coarse grains. The Vulcan wheat crop will average 20 to 25 bushels, the coarse grain crop probably 40. That means about 2,500,000 bushels of grain will be harvested there this fall.
No wonder there's such a rush all over the land to put up farm storage facilities.
Meantime farmers are going into debt. That is a report from Alberta, and it is not a Social Credit report.
Then here is a letter right off the firing line in southern Saskatchewan. It was not written for the perusal of government authorities, but was written as a friendly letter. Indeed, it was not even addressed to a member of parliament. This letter is dated October 2, 1953, and states:
You know they are drilling for oil south of town, and they hit oil yesterday. I don't know how much or what kind.
That is just introductory material. Then it continues:
We have had a grand fall; no rain, and the crops are all harvested, dry but can't sell any.
That does not sound very rosy, does it? Then a little farther down, he says:
Most people here have not sold a bushel this fall, and the businessman is left holding the bag. I have over $9,000 on the books, and the only excuse the farmer has for not paying is that he cannot sell any grain.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend at the moment to follow the hon, member who has preceded me by dealing with the situation prevailing generally on the prairies. Indeed, I had intended postponing any remarks on that question until we receive the decision by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) with reference to the suggestion made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) that a day be set aside for the discussion of that very important matter.
However, in view of the fact that there has been reference to it on one or two occasions during the course of the debate, later on in my remarks I shall make some reference to this very important matter, which affects not only the economy of the western provinces but also that of Canada as a whole.
It is always difficult to speak after an election, particularly when it does not turn out favourably for the party to which one belongs. I am not going to relive or revive any of the issues of that campaign. The Leader of the Opposition yesterday gave the lead when, in a most sportsmanlike way, he paid tribute to the Prime Minister and those associated with him in their victory.
However, having regard to the changed circumstances since the election, the farm situation, and the general loss of markets for agricultural products to which, up to now, several allusions have been made; and having in mind the general position in connection with textile manufactures and the like, perhaps I might be allowed to paraphrase the words of Sir Edmund Hillary who, describing his feelings when he had attained the summit of Mount Everest, said, "The view from the summit was not spectacular." It may well be that the government, looking over the situation and the changes that have taken place since the election, will admit that

Canada faces one of its most difficult periods. In consequence the responsibility of parliament becomes all the greater.
I am not going to relive that election campaign. We are in the opposition; we have our responsibility to discharge, to maintain our constitutional system. There can be no freedom without an opposition, strong and fearless to criticize, and above all to provide suggestions and ideas as an alternative to those advanced by the government.
I am sure that hon. members, and certainly the press of this country, after the election, realized the danger which is inherent in our constitutional system, when on repeated occasions one party achieves overwhelming power. There is one thing particularly that parliament must guard against-and it was perfectly evidenced in the decision made in connection with the Canadian Pacific Air Lines-namely, the philosophy that the big government knows best. That doctrine is a denial of representative government.
The responsibility of hon. members in all parts of the house is to make our democratic system operate. We in the opposition have a tremendous responsibility to examine in detail and to criticize with responsibility at all times the measures introduced by the government. I am one of those who believe that one of the major needs in our House of Commons is that provision be made at the expense of the state to place members of the opposition, who cannot have available to them the research facilities that are in such abundant measure accessible to the members of the government at all times, five or six trained experts in research technology, trade, agriculture and the like. Such facilities should be made available to Her Majesty's loyal opposition so that thereby members of the opposition may be placed in the position of being able to discharge properly, effectively and efficiently the functions and responsibilities resting on them.
Modern parliaments are very complex institutions. What a change there has been here since 1940, when I first entered parliament. Certainly no private member of parliament can, without technical assistance, discharge the responsibility that rests upon him in the extensive and ever-extending field of parliamentary discussion and decision.
I support the stand taken by the Leader of the Opposition when he suggested that estimates should be referred to a special committee, as has been done in recent years with the estimates of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson). Some say that to set up such committees would "strike at the root of ministerial responsibility." My 83276-71
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker answer is that ministerial responsibility in Westminster has not been undermined by establishing a similar system. The committee of the whole is totally unqualified, having regard to its numbers, to examine properly the estimates that come before parliament. I believe that, in the interests of efficiency and good government, something in the nature of or analogous to the system followed in Westminster, the mother of parliaments, should be put into effect here so that a committee similar to the public accounts committee of the United Kingdom might be set up under the chairmanship of a member of the opposition, meeting in secret, far from the fanfare of political partisanship, where estimates could be examined in detail with care and deliberation.
This parliament is young. Many young men were elected to parliament in the recent election. That is what makes parliament live, young men, and women too, who, in the words of Arnold Toynbee "will not accept the inevitability of the present but will as adventurers help to form it."
I know quite well that there are many cynical criticisms of men in public life. The answer to such criticism is in the quality of members of this house, who must serve unselfishly, with an abiding conviction and with personal sacrifice, if this nation is to achieve its true destiny. When I hear people speaking of the alleged wrongs of politics and the shortcomings of public life my answer is that in the field of politics human and moral values are translated into practice; only in parliament can sociological concepts and technological advances be translated into effectuality for the public weal.
All of us were deeply appreciative of the speeches made by the mover (Mr. Holling-worth) and the seconder (Mr. Villeneuve) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I do not like to hear repetition in that regard, but each of those speeches represented something worth while in this parliament. What we have to do during the honeymoon period following an election is to refrain from rehashing and repeating the issues of the campaign.
Since the election certain salient events have taken place, and one of these is the denial of an air cargo route to Canadian Pacific Air Lines by the cabinet of Canada. The amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) brings into most effectual perspective a major issue facing our country. How far are we to go in this country along the road of state enterprise? Are we to be placed in the position where the future of Canada and its development is to be considered as the patrimony of the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the cabinet? Is

The Address-Mr. DiefenbaJcer private enterprise going to be given an opportunity to develop, to expand, within the necessary limitations imposed by the welfare of the state being the pre-eminent consideration? Is government to hold back northern development at a time of progress never before equalled?
Those are some of the things that suggested themselves to me when I listened to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) yesterday as he explained why the government did not grant a licence for what had been asked for by thirty chambers of commerce of various cities which would be affected by the granting of this licence.
Are we to be in the position where a paternalistic government adopting a new philosophy is able to say to those who would risk their capital, in effect: It won't be good for you to do that. There is a danger that you will lose money. If private enterprise is willing to enter this new and untried field, the risk is the risk of private enterprise and the loss is not suffered by the people of Canada.
The decision by the government has received more general criticism than any action taken in recent years. I have before me representations from various parts of the country affected. I have in my hand representations of the city of Prince Albert within the constituency of Prince Albert which I now represent. Incidentally, Mr. Speaker, that is one of the two constituencies in Canada that has twice been represented by a prime minister. Quebec East was represented by Sir Wilfrid Laurier and is now represented by the present Prime Minister. Prince Albert for a short time in 1896 was represented, under the name of Saskatchewan, by Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and for many years by the late Right Hon. Mr. Mackenzie King.
Prince Albert was affected by this matter and representations were made by the city through its mayor, Mr. John M. Cuelenaere, and by the Prince Albert board of trade, represented by Mr. David Dalziel. Their representations were to the effect that this route was necessary, that northern Saskatchewan and northern Canada lacked the services which Trans-Canada Air Lines did not meet and could not meet by its southern route. The brief from Prince Albert read in part as follows:
Mining and prospecting in the pre-Cambrian shield of northern Saskatchewan has undergone extensive developments during the past few years.
The brief mentions Uranium City and other mineral developments in northern Saskatchewan including the tremendous resources of uranium so necessary for our survival,


resources that are mined north of Prince Albert. The submission ends:
We therefore submit that it would be in the public interest to grant the application of Canadian Pacific Air Lines Limited for a licence to operate a trans-Canada air cargo service as applied for.
Flin Flon, the city of North Battleford, the city of Prince Albert and all northern areas in Manitoba and Saskatchewan are affected by the denial of a licence to C.F. Air Lines, by the denial of what in my opinion should have been granted. This decision is an arbitrary order difficult to understand. What is the air transport board for? Is it a puppet? The board heard evidence. It did not make an unequivocal recommendation because to do so would be to bring about a change in public policy; but every finding in that report by the air transport board indicated the necessity of this licence being granted in view of the expanding development in northern Saskatchewan, Alberta and Manitoba. The board heard evidence, as it stated:
Some thirty chambers of commerce representing Canada's major urban areas represented to the board, as did the provincial government of Manitoba and many municipalities, private organizations and corporations, that there was a need for greater development of all-cargo services in Canada. Some supported the application of Canadian Pacific Air Lines Limited while others merely spoke of the general need for such a service.
The board sat; it heard evidence; it reported; and, for some reason that has as yet not been explained, the cabinet decided that it is not in the public interest because it might mean that the applicant would lose money.
That is not the spirit that will build northern Canada. In the speech from the throne a worth-while effort is made in connection with the changes to be made in the Department of Resources and Development. On one hand, in the speech from the throne northern development is given additional impetus. On the other hand, and in the same speech, a denial is made of one way which would encourage great development taking place in the northern areas.
Sir, if ever there was a doctrine that is a negation of risk, enterprise, and future development, it is that enunciated yesterday by the Prime Minister, in effect that the government is afraid that it will not be in the public interest. The applicant might lose money in the enterprise which would mean an application for higher rates.
Mr. Speaker, that decision was the most retrograde that has ever been made in connection with the development of northern Canada. Conditions in the world demand that northern Saskatchewan provide much of the uranium required in the years ahead.

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker
Even now I hope that the government will give the matter reconsideration. It would be too much to ask that the government give parliament the opportunity of deciding this, for certainly members representing the northern parts of Canada in every province would, if they carried out the will of their constituents, demand the granting of the licence asked for, thereby assuring a development which will otherwise be denied or delayed.
The uranium potential of northern Saskatchewan is the second greatest in the world. The development of this and other resources should not be arrested by the autocratic desires of one or other member of the cabinet. Private enterprise should be given the encouragement the state can provide. A major need for northern Saskatchewan is a defence road which would assure that, should war come, the transportation of uranium and other minerals could not be cut off by enemy action.
We have been warned by one of the greatest authorities in Saskatchewan, Professor Mawdsley of the University of Saskatchewan, of the danger in which the continued production of these resources stands unless proper defence facilities are provided. I feel that the government should give consideration to building defence roads in the northern areas which would not only provide for continued expansion and further development, but would assure that in time of war transportation could not be cut off as the result of enemy activities. In peacetime such roads would do more to expand development in the provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan than anything else that could be done.
The great development at Flin Flon, in northeast Saskatchewan, the great development of uranium in the north, ask and demand a defence road. That a radar chain is being built is an open secret in northern Canada. When these measures are being taken and defence works are being built why, at the same time, should these areas not have transportation facilities provided by means of a defence road equally useful in time of war and in time of peace? In that northern development we in northern Saskatchewan are affected by the topography or geography which up to the present has made that development of less advantage to our province because the output goes into other provinces.
It is because I believe in the necessity for an economic redevelopment on the prairies that I press for action and bring to the attention of the house and the country once more the vast developments that are taking place. Canada's resources of uranium will
go far to spell the survival of freedom. Our titanium resources must be made readily available, without which there can be no jet aircraft of the kind that we look forward to as being possible within the next three or four years. The shield of freedom can be welded by the minerals that are available there.
While on the one hand the government recognizes the necessity for northern development, as evidenced by the recommendations placed in the mouth of the governor general for the setting up of a new department or at least for expanding the present Department of Resources and Development, on the other hand advance has been bridled by the action taken by the government in refusing to allow the northern parts of our country to have available to them those cargo freight facilities which Trans-Canada Air Lines is not able to provide, for its routes are three hundred or four hundred miles south of the areas which require freight facilities by air.
I re-emphasize to the government the need for doing something now, the need for realizing not only that the setting up of a new department or the expansion of an old department is a step in the right direction, but that in addition there is required air freight cargo facilities which, by the action of the cabinet, have been denied particularly to the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and northern Alberta. Most Canadians realize that in competition there is survival for us and our way of life; that competition spells the difference between the attainments of freedom-loving people and those who are dominated by the theory that the state is all powerful and its decision is always right.
Russia has tremendous resources. Yet, without the impelling motive of private initiative and enterprise, Russia finds herself in an inferior position to the NATO countries because they are driven by that thing that has something divine in its origin, namely the will and incentive that comes to free men.
Surely this is not the time for the cabinet of Canada to say that there should be a monopoly in an enterprise that the publicly operated T.C.A. has not undertaken as yet. Surely we do not believe that we should continue to spoonfeed the government institution that has not dared enter into the northern freight transportation field. Private enterprise is prepared to undertake a necessary field of service but is denied the opportunity. While the request has been refused

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker for the time being, I suggest that "the time being" be of short duration so we shall soon be able to say that shortly the decision will be reversed and the right given to Canadian Pacific Air Lines to do that which Trans-Canada Air Lines has not undertaken up to the present and which is so necessary for our northern development.

The small farmer in western Canada finds himself in a difficult position. He realizes something of the world situation. He realizes that Canada has a large amount of surplus wheat on hand. He appreciates the fact that the United States has over 1,728 million bushels of wheat and requires only 700 million bushels for its own consumption. He


realizes that Canada will carry over some 352 million bushels this year, and he is greatly concerned about the disposal of that surplus. He can read the speech from the throne and he will find nothing in it to assist in solving his problem. The throne speech in effect avers that everything is fine but there is a surplus of wheat.
What are the government going to do? What are their trading plans? The United States has its plan for the disposal of certain surpluses, whereby approximately $250 million worth of surplus farm products may, under negotiations now being conducted with the British government, be sold to Britain. What are the plans of this government? What hopes are they holding out to the farmers that this surplus will be a benefit to mankind instead of being a detriment to Canadians? In the speech from the throne there is nothing to indicate government plans. There is not a word of hope, not a suggestion of a promise, but simply a reference in a casual sort of way to the situation.
I realize that it is a difficult problem, as do Canadians generally. No one wants to place the people of Canada in an impossible position. When he was in Winnipeg on October 28 the minister indicated that he was opposed to any system of loans. The distribution of money that was made from the 1952 pool has not met the situation. I know of the difficulties in connection with storage, and they were suggested by the Minister of Agriculture in the question asked a moment ago of the hon. member for Lethbridge. But, sir, within reasonable limits is there not something the government can work out in co-operation with the lending institutions whereby loans within proper proportions will be made available, based on the security of the wheat that is in the farmer's fields or in his granaries? I say to the Canadian people that there is no danger of loss in such a policy because no farmer can sell a bushel of wheat unless he has his permit book.
A loan system must be introduced in the interests of the small farmer, in the interests of the local businessman and retailer who finds himself in the position today of being unable to continue financing the local farmer. Surely there is some suggestion forthcoming from the government that will afford a little hope to these farmers.
What about granary space? I understand that the department of farm management of the University of Saskatchewan has estimated that the cost of new granaries for farmers would be 19 cents per bushel, without taking into consideration farm labour and materials. Incidentally, they have also indicated that the loss on protected field

storage on wheat would amount to 8-7 per cent per year, and on unprotected field piles to 10-1 per cent. Has the government something in mind that has not brightened the pages of the speech from the throne? Is there not something the government intends to do?

I should also like to extend my congratulations to the Deputy Speaker whose election also was a source of gratification to all, and it is with real sincerity that I pay the traditional compliment to the mover (Mr. Hollingworth) and the seconder (Mr. Ville-neuve) of the address. May I, as a private member, extend my sincere congratulations to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. (Laurent) upon the result of the August election. Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasant tradition in the house that, in this debate, private members may take their time to present glowing pictures of the beauties of their districts. Representing as I do one of the largest in the country, and definitely the best, the temptation is very great for me to do the same. However, unfortunately I have come to the conclusion that forty minutes is not long enough to do justice to the subject.
The new aluminum development now coming to fulfilment at Kitimat, with the power

development at Kemano, is in itself a subject which has been the material for many forty-minute speeches. The subject has been so well covered by magazines and periodicals in practically all parts of the North American continent that I am confident every member in the house knows as well as I do how important is this new aluminum project to Canada.
And so, instead of describing the many advantages of the riding of Skeena, I shall instead take a few moments to put before the house and the government some little problems which have arisen in that district, and most if not all of which I feel may be common to other similar districts across Canada.
Apparently a majority of the people of the country agree with me that we have a pretty good government. But, believe it or not, even this government is not always perfect, and some little sins of omission will sometimes crop up. That is only natural; after all, that is one of the reasons for our being here, namely to draw the attention of the authorities to those things which have not been done and should have been and, perhaps in a few cases, those things which have been done but should not have been done.
I have one particular instance in mind which I shall lay at the door of the Post Office Department. There is in that department a comparatively new procedure whereby, in a new community which has, we will say, grown up around one operation such as a fish cannery, one logging concern or one mine, the Post Office Department may decide that, while it will authorize a post office, the concern carrying on the operation shall assume full financial responsibility for the running of the post office.
I submit it is a good thing for every department of government, including the Post Office Department, to protect and to save so far as possible the money of the taxpayers of Canada. I would urge, however, that in this instance this unfortunate decision is based upon a wrong premise. When a post office is set up anywhere in Canada it is not set up for the benefit of one business concern carrying on operations in that locality. It is set up for the benefit of every Canadian who is resident in that locality, and who is entitled to obtain and to send mail.
I am sure I could come here to Ottawa and present to the government a new community with five separate industries each employing 15 people, thus making a new community of about 75 people; and in those circumstances Canada would supply a post office at the expense of the taxpayers. Then, if we have one community with perhaps four or five 53276-8
The Address-Mr. Applewhaite hundred people, is it fair that the post office should be supplied at the expense of the employer simply because those four or five hundred people happen to be on the same payroll?
I have no torch to carry for any particular employer; but I think perhaps it is not surprising to find that the opening of a post office is somewhat delayed when that is the position. So I would ask the government to remember that five hundred people working for one employer are just as much entitled to post office facilities at the public expense as are 500 people who may be distributed among five or six employers. I submit respectfully that this should be a self-evident proposition.
I should like to say a few words about search and rescue. I can speak about this subject only as it applies to the Pacific coast, because that is the only place where I have had any connection with it. Search and rescue is sometimes described as a coastguard service, because in the United States of America as well as in Alaska, with which I am more familiar, those services are carried out by the United States coastguard service.
I have two criticisms in this connection, one of which is that, with all due respect, I do not think we are doing as much as we should, and the other-and for this the government and the authorities are responsible-that we are doing a great deal more than is realized by the people.
Search and rescue on the Pacific coast is particularly applicable to marine and air losses. Both ships and aircraft get into difficulties and dangers, and sometimes disappear. The same applies on some occasions to individuals. Hunters, prospectors and tourists will occasionally get lost, upon which occasions the search and rescue service is brought into operation.
I know it would be very popular with my people at home if I were to ask for an unlimited expenditure on search and rescue. Even in respect of that service I do not think one is entitled to ask for too much. I do believe, however, that it is proper to ask for everything it is reasonably possible for Canada to provide, particularly in the light of the fact that, not only in that part of Canada but in all other parts, the population is on the increase. A service provided today for an area in which there are 20,000 people will be supplying 30,000 people in that same area in a few years.
Along the northern part of the coast in particular we find either that the search and

The Address-Mr. Applewhaite rescue service is not as efficient as it should be, or that it is not sufficiently familiar to the marine and aviation people. The result is that they do not know what protection is available.
Both those situations should be corrected. I submit that the most satisfactory and complete service which could be given on the northern part of the British Columbia coast would be the establishment at Prince Rupert or, if it were felt more feasible, on the Queen Charlotte islands, of not only a naval division such as we have at Prince Rupert, but the equivalent of a fleet air arm. I would like to see that supplied with helicopters for search and rescue purposes primarily. My submission is that the training and experience personnel would get in operating those helicopters, in providing search and rescue service, would certainly be of very great value if the navy were required to take part in operations for which it was originally formed, namely combat service.
This gives me an excuse to draw the attention of the house to the reserve naval division at Prince Rupert known as H.M.C.S. Chatham. It is worthy of consideration on many grounds, not the least of which is its proven efficiency. I can assure hon. members it is some satisfaction to me to be able to point out to the house that, as at June 30 last, the standings across Canada for the naval division efficiency trophy indicated that H.M.C.S. Chatham at Prince Rupert rated 127-7 points, whereas the next highest rated 47-18. Therefore I believe I am quite justified in saying that we have stationed there a most efficient naval division, which could be of inestimable value if it were supplied with aircraft of some kind or another for search and rescue purposes.
The Royal Canadian Air Force does not maintain a base right in my district. However, it has been most co-operative and has rendered extremely good service in the matter of search and rescue, and it is only right that it should be given credit for that service. Figures I have for the calendar year 1952, and which I believe to be correct, show that in the Pacific area alone in that year the R.C.A.F. took part in search and rescue missions in the following manner: 12 aircraft cases; 13 marine cases; 23 mercy flights, and 8 miscellaneous cases, including missing persons, making a total of 56 cases, involving 389 flying hours. Incidentally, in the whole of Canada during last year the R.C.A.F. took part in 222 search and rescue operations for a total of 5,453 flying hours.
That is not a bad record, and I suggest it does prove that Canada is not entirely asleep in the matter of search and rescue. But I am wondering whether the Royal Canadian Air

Force, the Royal Canadian Navy and all government vessels are as properly and efficiently tied together as they should be to give us a search and rescue service. I said "all government vessels". I refer not only to the fisheries vessels, the R.C.M.P. and the Indian affairs vessels under the jurisdiction of Canada, but also to the government vessels owned and operated by the province of British Columbia.
If-and I think this is likely-there is on paper or in effect a system whereby these vessels and planes are all available for search and rescue, then I wonder whether we have done our duty in telling the marine and flying commercial people on the coast what is available. I also wonder whether we have not made another little mistake. Have we told the people where they can send their calls of distress? Have we slipped up somewhere so that these calls of distress do not get distributed as widely as they should, so that what is available in the area does not get called as quickly as possible? I do not say that we have; I am not sure that we have not. Therefore one of the criticisms I have to make is that we do not know enough about what is being done.
I should also like to volunteer a suggestion which I think has merit, but which I would approach with an open mind. Many of our cases on the coast have to do with aircraft loss. I got very intimately mixed up with two of them this summer. One was rather spectacular and the other involved the loss of a personal friend of mine for whom I felt particularly responsible, as I had had something to do with his obtaining a licence to operate in the air. The suggestion I am going to make in this connection is that the proper authorities get in touch with local commercial air companies who employ a goodly number of bush pilots, men with an intimate flying knowledge of the area, men with an intimate knowledge of the habits of each other, who would know where a missing man would most likely be because they know what routes he would follow, and so on.
I should like to see these commercial fliers, every one of them, irrespective of whether they fly for a large company such as C.P.A. or a small outfit flying one plane, given a certain amount of authority and the right to exercise a certain amount of initiative, but particularly, with respect to the little fellows, not at their own expense. Perhaps some government supplies could be based centrally so any pilot who heard of a plane missing in that area could go as a matter of right, and take them, whether they were collapsible rubber boats, food, first aid equipment and

parachutes, or anything they might think was necessary because, particularly in the case of lost aircraft-it is so obvious that it need not be said-speed is a matter of great importance, and more particularly should a plane be down at sea. Therefore I am going to ask the authorities responsible for search and rescue to give that particular suggestion immediate investigation, because I believe it has merit.
Another matter of an entirely different nature to which I should like to refer-and here again it is going to call for some increased government expenditures-is the absolute necessity for something in the nature of a living allowance-whether you call it northern allowance or a special cost of living bonus or what, I do not care-for federal civil servants in areas such as the district of Skeena, where the prevailing wages are scores of percentage points above what they are across Canada. Our civil servants have been asking for that for some considerable time.
I would not want to give the wrong impression. They have not received the brush-off, but they have not yet received what we today consider a satisfactory acceptance of their request. Some time ago I received a communication-I have several of them, and I will quote only part of one-from the amalgamated civil servants of Canada, Miller Bay local council. Miller Bay, I should tell the house, is an Indian health service hospital operated a few miles from Prince Rupert. I want to read to the house two paragraphs from their submission and then endorse them. The paragraphs are:
We feel that conditions that fail to attract a high calibre of employees and result in a lowered standard are having, and will increase to have, a serious bearing on the future efficient and economical operation of the government's business.
Outside employers are offering greater opportunities, salaries, and conditions to efficient and trained personnel. This has, and is resulting, in an ever-increasing number of resignations of the best and more experienced people in the service. These people are being replaced by employees who are, in many cases, incapable of obtaining good employment in outside industry.
In other words I base my argument not so much-though perhaps that is justified-on asking that our people receive more money, but on the absolute necessity of giving our employees more money if we are not to lose them to private industry and have to accept only the type of employees whom private industry do not regard as worth more money, and the final end of that situation of course would be most unfortunate for the dominion.
I am glad to say that the speech from the throne mentioned housing. I should like to 83276-8J
The Address-Mr. Applewhaite lay before the house one little suggestion in connection with houses. It might be a somewhat local situation, nevertheless it is important. I have discussed the matter of housing at great length with veterans of my area and with particular reference to the Veterans Land Act. Let me make it clear there is not in Prince Rupert, nor within 50 miles of Prince Rupert, any arable soil. We are not a farming community; we are basically a fishing community, and our terrain is rock and muskeg. There is provision in the Veterans Land Act whereby a fisherman can take advantage of it. I am not speaking of the fisherman at the moment; I am speaking of the veteran, irrespective of his employment.
The veterans come to me and they say: "It is impossible-" and it is physically impossible- "for me to acquire in the Prince Rupert area the acreage necessary to qualify under the small holdings provision of the Veterans Land Act." I endeavour to point out what I will say to the house at the moment, that the small holdings provision was intended to enable the veteran to augment his income a little by growing some of his own vegetables or producing his own eggs, and so on; and that you cannot do in the area I am talking about. But whether it is done under the Veterans Land Act or some other act, I would urge that for the veterans'-I am discussing that one angle of the problem at the moment- a provision at least similar to the small holdings provision under the Veterans Land Act be made whereby they can acquire a home, not an apartment, similar to the homes which veterans can acquire if they are fortunate enough to live in areas which are arable.
As I say, I admit that there is a conflict of principle between the Veterans Land Act and the assisted houses, but a conflict of principle or difficulty of administration should not alone be any reason for this house not finding a satisfactory solution.
Another matter which arises in the district is entirely different, and this I imagine is pretty well peculiar to my area. My halibut fishermen, except the ones with small ships, fish far afield. They fish very largely in the gulf of Alaska and in northern waters. Those of you who are familiar with the map of the Pacific coast of Canada will realize that the Alaska panhandle comes halfway down the coast. I am told, and I believe it is correct, that where a fisherman has to put into a foreign port-in my case an Alaskan port- for emergency repairs, he is only entitled to bring those emergency repairs back to Canada free of duty if it was impossible-and that is the word, "impossible"-to get the ship back to a Canadian port without those repairs. Those who are familiar with halibut fishing

The Address-Mr. Applewhaite on the Pacific coast realize that halibut fishing lasts about 30 or 31 days. If a ship requires repair and has to come back from the gulf of Alaska to a Canadian port it is liable to lose from one-fifth to one-third of its whole year's catch. One-third to one-fifth of our halibut season is only from six to ten days.
The provision has another disadvantage in that it rather encourages ship owners to take chances. They are asked to bring their ship a matter of 400, 600 or 800 miles to a Canadian port instead of doing what one should do when thinking of life and limb; that is running to the nearest port to get repairs. I do not think it is the intention of this parliament, for the sake of a few dollars in duty, to force any bona fide fisherman to lose from one-third to one-fifth of his year's catch. Neither do I think it is our intention to force him to take unnecessary risks. I notice that among other things listed as coming before us this year there are the amendments to the Customs Act. I would ask the minister responsible to give this plea serious consideration if it requires amendment to the act. It may be that the position of which I complain can be cured by amendment of the regulations only.
I have only one other matter that I wish to refer to, Mr. Speaker, and it is in connection with airports generally and one in particular. I wish to express my thanks to the minister and the Department of Transport for the assistance they have given us in making a preliminary survey in connection with the establishment of an airport for wheeled aircraft at Prince Rupert. It is an airport which is going to be built not only for the sake of the pride of the people of Prince Rupert, something which does not count for very much, but also because it will be the only Canadian airport on the mainland north of Vancouver which can serve the country. Further investigations will have to be made, naturally, before even the cost of such an airport can be arrived at. I would urge the department to make those investigations.
In connection with airports generally I think the time has come for Canada to adopt a policy in connection with air transport which I think we adopted many years before my time in connection with water transport; namely, that wherever a community requires, and really requires, air transport we should assist them to get it. After all, where a community on the coast has required marine transportation this government-and I do not mean this Liberal government but the government of Canada over the last sixty years-has not been too slow in providing the necessary wharves for

marine transportation. We have to realize that we are in an air age, and that the same facilities for air transportation will have to be provided within reason.
If I am not over my time I would like to say this, Mr. Speaker. I was greatly impressed by a speech made by Mr. Grant McConachie, the president of Canadian Pacific Air Lines, in which he urged that every little community should not ask for a great big airport. He said the country could not afford it; and besides, big airports are not going to be needed at every stopgap place. He said small ports should be built so that air buses can pick up the traffic, human or freight, at those little places and transport those persons or freight to major places. From there they may travel on main airliners across Canada.
I would ask that this house give the same consideration to requests for small airports as it has given in the past to many requests for wharves.

Mr. Speaker, first I want to echo the sentiments of those in this house who complimented you on your ascension to the throne. Having been in the house with you for some considerable time I am sure that you will go down in history as perhaps one of the best Speakers this house has ever produced. I look forward to being ruled out of order quite frequently.
In view of the fact that the C.C.F. subamendment points up the necessity for a national health program, I am just going to say a few words about it. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) made the case for a national health program very well and I have no intention of repeating it, as I have other matters to deal with. However, I would say that in my judgment the establishment of a national health program in this country is a must at the present time. I think 98 per cent of the people of this country would' back the government in bringing down something that would make medical science available to all the people of this country.
Conditions are very bad in that field. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) can stand up in his place and say that the government has spent a lot of money in building hospitals and providing more bed space, and that is quite correct. But they have not provided any way for the majority of the people of this country to occupy those beds. Those people cannot get into them. They cannot afford to do so. You are also still far short of bed space, and you do not have to leave this city for proof of that. I think right now you have perhaps 1,600 or 1,700 people

on the waiting list at one hospital, and perhaps 1,500 or 1,600 at another. Those are people who can afford the beds, but in many sections of this country I know there is bed space but people cannot afford to pay the $12 or $14 per day in order to secure the services.
The time has come when something has to be done about it, and I think even the medical profession is realizing that today. One of the most disorganized professions in Canada today is the medical profession. They are in a transition from the old to the new and they know that the new is going to come. For a good many years people with selfish interests have struggled against all progress. I am sure that the government realizes that.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I wish to bring something to your attention. Hansard of the last day of the last parliament will indicate that I asked the Speaker of this house, through the then minister of public works, if when the members returned to the next parliament -regardless of who came back-he would have a television set installed in room 16-

I shall be glad to answer that question. Room 16 is just outside this chamber. It is the members' room. It is a place where members can go and sit, listen to the radio, and meet their friends. It is a general recreational room provided for the members of the House of Commons. A lot of other things go on there, too.
Mr. Speaker, as most members of this house know, the throne speech debate is an omnibus affair and is largely designed to give members an opportunity to air the grievances of their own communities; and most of them take advantage of that opportunity. I
The Address-Mr. Gillis notice that considerable straw has been threshed already. At this time I am going to pose to this house a problem that I have brought before it a good many times, but I am going to do it in a little different way this time, because, despite all of the talking I have done about it, it has become worse and worse.
I am going to make two charges. I understand that is a good legal way of doing things, namely to charge people. Then after making those charges I am going to support them with documentary evidence or, as I think the lawyers would say, corroborative evidence. I am going to charge the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation of Canada-it is not only in Nova Scotia; it is an octopus that roams from coast to coast-with the sabotage of the coal and steel industry of eastern Canada.
That is a serious charge and I am going to prove it. I am going to charge the federal government with failure to protect the public funds they have put into that corporation. You have a statutory provision that appropriates $4 million a year for subvention purposes, and it is paid out. Some of it goes to the railways and a lot of it goes to the company. You have a $7J million investment by way of loan to the Dominion Coal Company. I am charging that the dominion coal board or the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys have not enforced the terms of the bill under which that money was loaned. That bill stated that the project for which the money was loaned must be economically sound, in the best interests of the community and sound from an engineering standpoint. I am charging that all three of those provisions were violated by the federal government, for the department responsible for the administration of that fund has not done anything about it.
The first thing we have to ask ourselves is this; and in doing this kind of thing I am in good company. I am in the company of the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Winters). I notice that at a recent convention in Halifax -he was addressing that Liberal association convention-he too made charges, according to this press dispatch, to the effect that the Intercolonial Coal Company operating in Westville, where about four thousand people are affected, had closed that mine without proving that it was necessary to close it because orders from the Canadian National Railways were still there to be filled and they would have continued that operation for at least four more months, but the company just closed it down. The minister made that accusation before that body. There is a press

The Address-Mr. Gillis dispatch here to that effect, and it is quite recent. I am therefore in good company. That is corroborative evidence.
The first thing we have to prove is this: What about that resource? Has it run out? Is there any coal there? Can it be mined successfully? It is necessary to go back a little way, in my judgment, in order to show what is a gradual, deliberate breakdown of the industry by the company itself. I have here in my hand a copy of the minutes of a special House of Commons committee on reconstruction and re-establishment. I was a member of it. We sat here for some considerable time. These minutes are volume No. 2 of Wednesday, March 17, 1943. On the question as to the resource itself, how much coal is there, the witness on that day was Dr. F. W. Gray, assistant general manager, Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation of Sydney, Nova Scotia; and by the way, he is also a geologist. On the question as to what resources were there and what could be done about them he said this, and I quote from page 26 of these minutes:
I and my boy, who is a geologist, made a very -lose study of that field. We spent together probably about eight years on the study, and I came to :he conclusion that in the Sydney coal field we can produce at about the same rate of output for the next, say, 180 years. That takes into account the question of mining submarine coal and the changes of quality and the persistence in the seams. I think that district offers a possibility of mining, say, five million long tons of coal a year over almost two hundred years. So from the point of view of post-war reconstruction there is no question about the resources, at least so far as Cape Breton is concerned, and more particularly the Sydney coal field.
One hundred and eighty years' supply there! Would produce five million tons a year perhaps for the next 200 years! Let us see what has happened to that industry since. To give you some idea of the importance of the industry to Nova Scotia from the standpoint of dollars here is a little quotation from another official document:
Last year coal production in Nova Scotia was estimated at 6,600,000 short tons as compared with 6,412,113 in 1949. Total mineral production in the province was valued at approximately $60 million last year, of which coal accounted for some $51 million.
So in terms of mineral dollars that industry is extremely important. Let us take a look at the dominant position occupied in that province by that huge corporation that is sometimes referred to in this house as free enterprise. I should like to know who is competing. Dosco employs about 30,000 people, over 16,000 of whom work in Nova Scotia and nearly 2,000 in the iron mines in Newfoundland. The rest work in the central

Canadian plants of the corporation. Approximately 75,000 men, women and children in Nova Scotia are directly dependent on Dosco for a livelihood. That is nearly one-sixth of the population of the province. The areas and towns that are completely dependent on Dosco contain a population of about 130,000 or somewhat over 20 per cent of the entire population of the province.
When you are talking about that organization and its effect on the economy and the lives of the people of that province, you are not airing a grievance; you are making a plea for a reorganization of the economy of the province. It is drastically upset at the present time. What is the reason for this? Why is our coal industry declining? In my judgment it is because the company is no longer interested in mining and selling coal except for their own requirements in the Dosco steel plant at Sydney.
I charge the federal government also with being slack in permitting that corporation to set up in Montreal a wholly-owned subsidiary that is importing United States coal and selling it in the Montreal and Ontario markets and backing the industry in Nova Scotia completely out of the picture.
Let us see what influences may be at work. In my judgment United States capital coming into this country is gaining control of our natural resources to the extent that it is folding them up and marketing its own products in Canada. That is what is happening with respect to coal. Maybe the miners' union was not far astray in a brief they presented to the federal government on June 6, 1948. This organization has a good research department too, and this is what they had to say as found on page 6 of the brief. Incidentally, there will be a copy of the brief in the office of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham). They said:
Further decisive evidence of the manner in which the steel plants of the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation can be expanded, of the urgent need for an inquiry to establish this and of the strong probability that national and provincial interests demand immediate investigation is provided by certain recent developments. There is now ample evidence indicating that American interests control or may shortly control Dosco's huge steel and coal empire.
This was in 1948.
The American Securities Corporation, 25 Broad street, New York, has acquired since its formation in 1946 what we understand is a substantial interest in Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation Limited. Mr. Charles G. Terry, president of American Securities Corporation and chairman of the finance committee of Colorado Fuel and Iron Corporation, is now a director of Dosco. Mr. R. J. Wysor, past president of Republic Steel Corporation, has also received a similar appointment to Dosco's board.

These appointments were in 1948, and the buying into Dominion Steel and Coal company by United States interests took place in 1946. Since 1948 up to the present time the production of steel has not expanded in the maritime provinces. At the present time some 600 men have been laid off in the steel plant, and the coal mines are folding up. I am wondering if it is not because the United States interests have sufficient control today to hold back and scrap the Canadian industry in order to market their own product in this country.
I have a photostatic copy of an advertisement here that sounds rather ridiculous for a Canadian coal company to be putting out. It is a very large advertisement in the Montreal papers and it says:
This year tell your customers to heat with the best eastern Kentucky Elkhorn coal.
That advertisement is signed by the Dominion Coal Company Limited. That company is advertising Kentucky coal in their own economic market, the Quebec markets, when they are closing up their own mines.

Certainly; there is no doubt a lot of it would be used for that purpose. That definitely proves that the company has no intention of mining coal with the exception of what it may need for the steel plant. Here is another clipping saying "Prince Edward Island dealers are buying United States coal". Why should they be buying it? It is because they cannot get coal from Cape Breton, so they are importing United States coal and bringing it all the way to Prince Edward Island. It is being sold in Prince Edward Island because the Dominion Steel and Coal company is not even supplying its own local market. Does that not look as if the Yanks had the inside track? It certainly does to me.
Ottawa is doing its share to cut coal out. Another newspaper dispatch indicates that no more coal is to be used at Rideau Hall. The Governor General made a trip to my part of the country a few weeks ago. I was on a few platforms with him. He took a look at the mines, his heart bled for the miners, he was sympathetic, but he came right back, cut coal out and put in oil. That was a practical way of demonstrating his sympathy; and this was only a few weeks ago.
On the other hand I find that another newspaper report indicates that more coal is
The Address-Mr. Gillis en route to South Africa. Ships are coming into Sydney, loading our coal and taking it all the way to South Africa and Brazil, where it is being manufactured into nylons which are then being sold in Canadian and United States markets. Why can we not manufacture them? Where is this great free enterprise, this risk capital and all this competition? United States interests are crossing the border and buying up our resources; and he who has economic control of this continent in the next ten years will run it. We have sold our iron ore deposits to them and we have sold our coal industry to them. They are forcing our industries to close, they are taking over the country, and most of us have not brains enough to see it. One of these days we will wake up with an American military dictatorship wrapped around our necks.
Unemployment in that part of the country is double what it was at this time last year, according to the latest figures from the unemployment insurance commission. What is it doing to these communities? There was no gradual lay-off of people in the mining communities. The general manager of Dominion Coal issued an arbitrary order over the radio closing down a certain colliery. The fact that some 1,400 men were unemployed there and that their families and the whole community, with hospital, schools and so forth, were involved did not make any difference. There was no consultation with anyone. He just said: the mine is finished; it is closed.
Another announcement came only a few days later, making 400 more unemployed. In the particular area that the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. McCulloch) represents every mine has been completely closed. I heard someone from British Columbia say their mines are also closed but that their men have gone into other industries. That is also true in Alberta, but in Nova Scotia there is no other industry. They just sit there. They are on unemployment insurance. The figure for unemployed in that mining area alone is 2,900, but that is only about half the total. That represents those who are registered and who are receiving unemployment insurance. Anyone not in receipt of unemployment insurance is not represented in that figure, and the total is double that.
Unemployment insurance will last a year or nine months for some of them. What happens after that? Where do they go from there? It amazes me to hear hon. members ask for more relief for India, Africa and China because, although I agree with that, charity begins at home. I think the first responsibility
112	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Cillis of both the provincial and federal governments is to the people of our country, the miners who are out on the street, the steel workers who are being thrown out of work today.
A large percentage of them are boys who donned the uniform and fought for Canadian institutions. They did not do so to come back and stand on the street and live on unemployment insurance or on nothing when unemployment insurance runs out. The part of the country for which they fought is the part in which they live and have their homes. They have built their homes and communities there. Ninety-eight per cent of these people own their own homes, and if they leave there they cannot sell them. Property values are down. If they go to Ontario, Quebec or British Columbia they cannot find a home in which to live. Therefore they are stuck.
I think it would be a good idea for the immigration service to take a look at the unemployed in these areas of the maritimes and determine if it is not possible for the Canadian government to at least treat them as well as the people we are taking in from Europe. We grant such people a year's hospitalization and so on. We give money to the provinces to subsidize their education, but nothing is done for people who for years and years have paid their taxes. They build communities, they maintain hospitals, and overnight there is an arbitrary decision on the part of one of those great democrats in the field of free enterprise who can tell you that you are through working. He who controls your job controls your life under this present scheme of things.
Let us take a look at what happened with respect to hospitals. There are two good standard hospitals in the town of Glace Bay. These hospitals were built by the miners and maintained by them on a subscription basis. Each one of these men paid a dollar a week, which provided hospitalization for them; but with this present lay-off-well, I have a few figures here for one of the hospitals. The closing of 1-B and No. 24 collieries has resulted in the loss of $4,000 per month since June of this year. Income from their subscriptions for the months of March, April and May of this year amounted to $51,927.34. Income from the same service for the months of July, August and September amounted to $39,102.59, a difference of $12,824.75.
In the meantime monthly expenses have remained the same, because they had not curtailed service to the subscribers who were laid off. However, due to the fact they had no reserve funds of any kind this loss of


revenue was reflected in the amount owed the bank each month. Furthermore, the hospital is faced this year with a portion of the cost of repairing the buildings. This will probably amount to something between $12,000 and $20,000. They are trying to carry on but if something is not done to assist a hospital in that position it will have to close. It cannot carry on in that way, and the other hospital in that town is in the same situation. Sydney is finding itself in the same position as a result of closures.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am going to say this. I think the situation in our natural resources in this country, not only in coal alone but in iron ore-iron ore is basic, as steel is basic, to the whole economy of the country-is worth investigating. Steel runs into everything. It is in all your kitchen utensils. He who controls steel on this continent in the future is going to control the North American continent. We have sold our iron ore resources to United States interests. There is no doubt about that. They are moving in on these resources and they are pushing our coal out of the picture. They are marketing their coal in this country.
I have just shown you that Dosco has very big United States financiers on the board of directors. I am beginning to wonder who is running that organization. It certainly is not being run for the benefit of Canadians. We import billions of dollars worth of steel from the United States, yet there is a basic steel industry down there that has done little except modernize and has made no planned extensions whatever. Right today this industry is laying off between 500 and 600 men at that Sydney plant.
I think the time has come, Mr. Speaker, when a commission or someone else in this country should take an inventory of our resources and ascertain exactly what is happening. We should find out who is running the show. I think the situation today is serious enough for the government to use the Emergency Powers Act. This is one time this act could be used, for this is a dire emergency for a whole province because the very foundation of our economy has been removed. If you declared a state of emergency there you could go in and find out what is wrong. You have some responsibility, at least some social responsibility, and you have the responsibility of protecting the investment you have in that industry.
The company have shown quite definitely that they have no social responsibility. They tear up communities just by arbitrary decision announced over the radio. No one lifts a

finger to do anything about it. The government leases these properties and allows someone to tear them up without any regard for future generations. I think the government should at least take a look at the picture and find out just what is happening to our resources in this country. If I were on that side of the house I would certainly say this is one time we could declare a state of emergency, at least in that province.
Let us examine the coal and steel industry, but not as that royal commission did with a whitewash report and a rehash of old resolutions and evidence that I saw thirty years ago. There was nothing new in that report, not even a new recommendation, except the recommendation to set up the coal board and that recommendation was contained in the minority report. The coal board is all right but it does not work, and perhaps it is not allowed to work.
I have suggested a good many times in this house that the coal industry should be declared a national industry. It should be brought under the coal board right from east to west. This board has the responsibility of developing markets. It could do it, but it is not doing a very good job when one sees United States coal being imported into Prince Edward Island and Dosco being permitted to import United States coal into our economic market in the province of Quebec. It is certainly not doing much about markets. It is time someone woke up and tried to do something.
Coal is not out of the picture yet, Mr. Speaker. The time will come when you are going to need the coal industry, so it should not be scrapped. There is no assurance as to how long gas and oil will last, and if we run into an emergency such as the last war, where you were pouring oil into war machines all over the world, you will certainly need coal in this country as a standby.
According to a press dispatch an eminent authority states that the coal industry has yet to reach its peak. It will come back. That is this man's judgment. Here is another peculiar thing. While we are scrapping our own industry, a press dispatch of recent date from Victoria, British Columbia, states that United States interests are launching a survey in British Columbia and Alberta in order to locate good coal fields. They are going to develop a coal field or use a good coal project in British Columbia and perhaps in Alberta.
Why do we not develop it? These interests will find a market for that coal. While we are scrapping our own industry they will come in and set up an industry in British Columbia and Alberta, and they will sell
The Address-Mr. Gillis Canadian coal to Canadians through United States interests. If the Yanks are coming here in search of coal would it not be a good idea to maintain our own resources?
I am strongly urging the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) that the time has come to extend the Unemployment Insurance Act. I see no ray of hope for the employment of these men in that part of the country. Many of them have come seeking advice. They were going to go to Ontario, but I said, "No, do not go to Ontario, Quebec or anywhere else; you cannot run away from life. You might as well fight here as anywhere else. With the falling off of our defence program, perhaps in another six months Ontario and Quebec may be worse off than we are from the standpoint of unemployment, and if you are going to be unemployed and are going to live on unemployment insurance you had better be in your own home where the landlord cannot charge you $150 and kick you out the first time the rent is not paid. Live in your own home, form committees and live off unemployment insurance." If the federal and provincial governments have not enough imagination and interest to develop something in the way of subsidiary industries, or to protect the coal and steel industry, then perhaps we can do it ourselves.
There is a chain of finance in this country that was made possible by a bill introduced at the last session which established a national credit assistance act linking up all the credit unions across this country. That enabled them to lend money in other provinces, and we have a committee at the present time studying the potential of Cape Breton island, particularly as to what can be done by way of subsidiary industry. Perhaps we can set up a plate mill down there. We threw away the one we had that was built by taxpayers' money. There are many things we can do. The committee is studying that matter now. Possibly it could' be financed on a co-operative basis, and we could run the show ourselves. A great number of our people think along those lines. Once you begin to build something yourself you will find others who will try to set up something to offset it.
I am making only these two requests. I would ask the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham) to make an examination into what is going on in the Dominion Coal Company, to find whether the terms of the bill under which that loan was made are being carried out. Second, I am suggesting to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) that he discuss with his officials the

The Address-Mr. Maltais possibility of extending unemployment insurance to cover the period these people in that area may be unemployed; because if something like that is not done the picture looks very bleak indeed for that part of Canada.
