speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to offer you my most sincere congratulations on your appointment as Speaker of this house. Your well-known sense of fairness and your experience in the enforcement of the rules of the house surely qualified you as candidate for that high office.
(Text):
I should like for a few moments to speak in the English language, if in doing so I am not out of order. I deliver this portion of my remarks in English because at this time I should like to refer to the last electoral campaign. I shall be as brief as I can. May I point out that during that campaign some of us were visited by opposing speakers, the result of which was that I tried to work even harder to prove to my constituents that I was supporting the right party in my quest for victory.
Among those who visited my part of the country was the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees). The incident to which I shall refer took place on a pleasant Sunday morning. Those who were privileged to make the trip down the Saguenay last year will realize how charming and peaceful is the St. Lawrence. During the campaign I followed the procedure of having people listen on my behalf to what was being said against me or the policies of the government I was supporting, so that I might answer. On the Sunday morning in question the hon. member for Broadview spoke at a rally supporting the Progressive Conservative candidate. It was reported to me by those people who listened to the hon. member, and reported also by the press, that he made the statement that the Progressive Conservative party was going to take office; that in doing so it would name an envoy to the Vatican and-I am stating what appeared in the newspapers-that the French language would be used on the same level as English in the printing of bills, and that there would be established a national flag.
I was greatly surprised to learn all this, but I told my constituents that they need not place much trust in those promises because that party was not going to be returned to power. It was with some surprise that I read in the issue of the Toronto Daily
[Mr. Gillls.l
Star of July 28 the following heading: "George Hees denies saying Tories would name envoy."
I was busy with many other duties at the time, so I did not have the opportunity to check as to the accuracy of this newspaper clipping, or as to whether the hon. member for Broadview really meant what he said. I felt that I would have an opportunity during this debate to find out from him whether he did make that statement, whether it is contrary to what he said in the constituency of Charlevoix, or whether he did not say anything about it.
As I listened this afternoon to the speech of the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) I noted that, in a few words in his remarks, he asked that his party be given the help of six or seven experts. Let me say that the Progressive Conservative party should feel happy that it has no experts. As I speak tonight about the housing problem I have before me a publication of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation, a publication prepared by experts; and I am not using it because it was prepared by experts. AH I could make out in it was the title and the last page. (Translation):
And now, Mr. Speaker, as I stated a while ago my remarks will deal more particularly with the National Housing Act and the pension for invalids.
It is said that the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne gives us the opportunity of setting forth some of the needs of the counties we represent, while it affords members of the opposition the opportunity of criticizing the government.
Being a member of the party that directs the destinies of the country, I hope I will be forgiven if I use these few minutes to say some good things about the government, because what happened last August surely shows that I am justified in doing so.
I still recall a famous debate of the 21st parliament, when the members of the house were voting huge sums of money for the defence of the country. I also recall the sacrifices that we then asked the Canadian people to make in order to establish that line of defence, that strong bulwark against Russian imperialism, a measure that has been justly called an insurance policy against any future war.
Now that the years have gone by, and that we are able to look back, we have reason to take pride in this action taken by the government. Recently, we have witnessed

a break in the open warfare in Korea, and we all hope that, as the President of the United States, in his recent visit here, seemed to have indicated, the allied nations will soon enjoy an era of peace and prosperity. I believe all that is the result of the action of the government which, when it was asking great sacrifices from the Canadian people, has managed to bring about amendments to the legislation which have helped our economy.
It is with pleasure that, as I was listening to the speech from the throne, I noted that the government proposed to empower the banks to place further sources of money at the disposal of the Canadian people, in authorizing them to lend money on mortgages. Frankly, I would have preferred that the government had given wider power to the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to enable it to grant what we call direct loans.
Since I have the honour of representing a rural constituency, I must admit quite frankly that I have not always agreed with the policy of the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. I remember full well the fights I had on my hands to obtain loans in certain rural districts.
The hon. member who seconded the address in reply (Mr. Villeneuve) the other day told of a father who was pointing out to his son that his country was the land in front of him, the family home. I agree with that. I too believe that for any individual the ownership of a piece of land constitutes a bond, something that causes him to appreciate more fully the advantages which a democracy is able to extend to its citizens.
We know there is a great deal to be done yet in this country in order to enable a large number of Canadians to become home owners. A few days ago I was reading a research bulletin put out by the Canadian Congress of Labour. It pointed out that more than
460,000	homes in Canada are in need of repair. It was also pointed out that many Canadians who would like to own their own homes are unable to do so because of lack of funds.
It is true that this new measure will increase the sources of mortgage loans, will help a large proportion of the population, but I wonder whether this will be of any benefit to the people. At the present time, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation
The Address-Mr. Maltais guarantees loans up to 80 per cent of the approximate value of a house under construction. Unfortunately, those who can afford the down payment, that is to say invest in such construction the initial amount required by the law, are not numerous. I believe it would be wise for the government to increase that guarantee of 80 per cent to 85 or 90 per cent. This has already been tried with respect to war workers, and I do not see why a similar plan could not be of help to the Canadian population regardless of occupation.
Still on this matter of the National Housing Act, sir, you will allow me no doubt to point out to you an incident, or rather to explain to you the circumstances which followed a fire in the county of Charlevoix.
I still remember with sadness the phone call I received, while parliament was in session in Ottawa, telling me that the municipality of St. Urbain was afire. I left Ottawa immediately and upon my arrival I discovered that about half of the village had been destroyed by fire. Fortunately, the victims of the fire did not lose heart; they went first to their municipal government, then to their provincial government and finally they asked me to get federal assistance for them.
I met the municipal authorities and explained to them the procedure to follow if they wanted to get some help from the federal government, for I knew at that time what was the government's policy in such matters. The established principle is that the federal government intervenes only when the provincial authorities are unable to do anything, and providing the disaster is of national importance. The proper procedure is to forward an appropriate request to the government of the province concerned. Such was the policy of the government and I do not believe it has been changed.
I had pointed out to the municipal authorities that it was advisable to submit their request through the provincial authorities. The tragedy occurred shortly before the provincial elections in Quebec and I do not know how closely that procedure has been followed. However, as far as I could ascertain, the federal government had received no request on that matter. I went back to tell my fellow citizens of St. Urbain that no request had been submitted to the central government. Other representations were then made asking [DOT] me if new attempts could not be made to get from the federal government an amount of money equal to that which had been given by

The Address-Mr. Maltais the provincial government to the victims of the disaster at St. Urbain. Unfortunately the procedure to be followed at the time of that disaster is still the same, as we found out following the fire that destroyed the parish of St. Neree in Bellechasse county. That is why when I think of those calamities, of those disasters which sometimes reach such large proportions that the individual upon whom they fall can no longer cope with them with his own resources, I wonder if it would not be appropriate to establish, here in Canada, what we would call a national relief fund to help those districts or those individuals who are sometimes victims of such calamities.
A couple of days ago I heard an hon. member ask the government if they intended doing something for those who had been victims of infantile paralysis, in Manitoba I believe. That is another typical case, where part of the population suffers from a calamity with which it cannot cope with its own income. To certain people perhaps the plan I am proposing may seem bold, but have we not, at the international level, what we call the Colombo plan, in other words a plan enabling the government to help the underprivileged nations.
I suggest that we should get together, here in Canada, and establish a special fund in order to give assistance as quickly as possible to the people of the districts struck by such calamities, for it is indeed' when one has gone through a misfortune, when one feels low and is at the end of one's resources, that help is needed, and these Canadians in distress should not have to wait for months and even years before being able to get the assistance that they need.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that it is important -in fact we are in duty bound to do so-to set up a national fund to this end. Then, should disaster strike once more such as has been the case at St. Urbain or St. Neree, we will be in a position to help these people without waiting for the passage of legislation or for the implementation of special procedures to this end.
I was also happy to note in the speech from the throne reference to the fact that the federal government intend to request provincial co-operation in helping invalids. There is nothing sadder than to walk into a home where one of the parents or one of the sons is sitting helpless on a chair because of a disability which has handicapped him or her

for life. These poor people, who are crippled through no fault of their own, are an imposition upon their family. They live in an atmosphere where morale is automatically affected. In the world as it is today I think that the state should help these invalids.
Since the government intends to ask for provincial co-operation in this matter, I do hope that it will go as far as to bring about a plan which will be acceptable, for I am one of those who have known the plight of these disabled. As a matter of fact, allow me to point out that often some blind people write to us to say that their pension is utterly inadequate and that the limit imposed on gains or income that they may earn apart from their pension is unfair.
It seems to me that we should show more humanity towards these disabled persons. I do hope that the provinces will be generous enough to work out some program whereby these disabled persons may have something to look forward to in life.
These were, Mr. Speaker, the few remarks I wished to make in this debate. There are other problems which concern the county I have the honour to represent; I intended to bring them to your attention but I think the opportunity will be more suitable when the estimates are under consideration later on during this session.

speechtext:
My
first words in this debate will be to congratulate the Speaker on his election in this twenty-second parliament. Those of us who had the opportunity of serving with the Speaker in the twenty-first parliament came to know the capable way in which he would carry out his duties, and I am sure that he will. rule this house with justice but still with firmness.
To those words I add my congratulations to you, sir, as Deputy Speaker of the twenty-second parliament. We of central Ontario, in which your constituency is located, are proud indeed that you have been honoured by your appointment.
I should like, as others have done, to congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I have been privileged to hear several of those addresses moved and seconded, but I am sure all of us who have heard such speeches before will concur in the statement that the mover and seconder did an outstanding and admirable job. Too, I am sure we should

congratulate the new ministers, the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) who has brought to the cabinet a wealth of background experience in policy making and administration; and also the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Lesage) who has served as a parliamentary assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs and to the Minister of Finance. He too has had a great deal of background experience, and I am sure both those gentlemen will add great strength to the cabinet.
I also congratulate the new parliamentary assistants: the parliamentary assistant to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pinard), the parliamentary assistant to the Postmaster General (Mr. Kirk), the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Robertson) and the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Bennett). I am sure it is of significance for me to point out that three of those new parliamentary assistants came from what was known as the "rump" group, the Liberal group which sat to the left of the Speaker. I think all who served in this rump group are particularly pleased that three of their members from the last parliament were so honoured as to be promoted to parliamentary assistants and the junior cabinet.
There are approximately 76 new members in this new parliament, I understand, and I am sure I may be pardoned if I take the opportunity of telling them something about the constituency of Hastings South, which I represent. This constituency is situated in the province of Ontario about 120 miles east of Toronto and 230 miles west of Montreal. It is bounded on the south by that great waterway, the bay of Quinte, formed into a bay by the county of Prince Edward. Now that the Murray canal which joins the bay of Quinte and lake Ontario on the west side has been a waterway for many years that county could almost be termed "Prince Edward Island" too.
The constituency of Hastings South, according to the last dominion census, has a population of 57,500 people. The constituency is about equally divided into urban and rural sections. It is bounded on the east by the town of Deseronto and on the west by the western limits of the town of Trenton. There are within this constituency the villages of Tweed, Point Anne, Frankford, Corbyville and Batawa. There are the towns of Deseronto and Trenton and, of course, the capital city of the county, the city of Belleville. Each urban centre plays a very important part in the life and economy of this community and, in turn, in the life and economy of this great
The Address-Mr. Follwell Dominion of Canada. At one time, when the package freighters were plying up and down the bay of Quinte and through the locks, the town of Deseronto was a bustling point. It was a manufacturing centre of woodenware and the centre of a great lumbering industry. That has gone by the boards. At Deseronto we now have a plant manufacturing electronics, and with the proposed development of the deep waterway system it is quite probable that in the near future the town of Deseronto will again be a very busy port on the lake front.
As I say, on the west we have the town of Trenton which this year celebrated its 100th anniversary. Also celebrated at Trenton this year was the 100th anniversary of King Street United Church. King Street United Church was built one hundred years ago, in 1853. Celebrated too with the town's centennial was the centennial of the only newspaper in Trenton, the Courier-Advocate.
Trenton, as I say, is fast becoming a manufacturing centre. Just a few short months ago the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) came to Trenton to officially open a branch of an English industry known as the Pyro-Tenax plant.
In the constituency of Hastings South there is a Royal Canadian Air Force station at Trenton, which is the largest air force station in the Dominion of Canada. During the war hundreds of commonwealth pilots were trained at this R.C.A.F. station at Trenton, and they went forward to make that great contribution which ended in victory for the free peoples.
This afternoon my hon. friend and colleague the hon. member for Hastings-Fron-tenac (Mr. White) spoke briefly in regard to the mineral developments in the county of Hastings. He mentioned the great iron ore development near Marmora which has been carried out by the Bethlehem Steel Corporation. At the present time there are approximately 500 men working on this project and it is estimated that there is sufficient ore to last at least 20 years. As he said, this ore was discovered by magnetometer on an aerial flight.
In the north end of the county at the present time there is great action with regard to uranium. Throughout the length and breadth of the county of Hastings there are mineral deposits, and over the years they have proved to be very good little industries. A few years ago gold development in the county was active, but it now has petered out. However, who knows what will be discovered in Hastings, as in any other part of this great dominion?

The Address-Mr. Follwell
Last evening, along with several other members of parliament, I had the opportunity of attending a meeting with the textile workers' union of America, at which was discussed the necessity of doing something for the sagging textile industry. Today the textile workers' union presented a brief to several of the cabinet ministers. I have received several telegrams from the textile workers in the town of Trenton in my constituency, and they have informed me that they are now working on short time, with not much prospect of improved conditions. However, I am sure all of us were highly gratified to hear the words of the cabinet ministers who attended the meeting today, which indicated that an amendment to the Customs Act is to be proposed with regard to dumping, in order to protect the textile industry, which has always been a great employer of labour and has made an outstanding contribution to the economy of this country.
I should like to join with those members who have already spoken in this debate with regard to the request by the Canadian National Institute for the Blind. I am sure it would be well to put on record part of the memorandum which was sent to the members on behalf of the blind in this country. It reads as follows:
In 1937, pensions for the blind were established, related to the old age allowances, all being subject to the means test. The blind were permitted an addition to the means test ceiling of $120 per annum, in view of additional living cost due to blindness. From time to time, rate of allowances and ceilings were raised, with proportionate increase in ceiling for both the blind and the aged.
In the legislation of 1951, effective January 1, 1952, the Old Age Pensions Act was superseded by the old age security legislation, with an allowance of $40 per month free from the means test. Coincidentally, the blind of 21-69 years of age were segregated from the old age group and afforded blindness allowance under the Blind Persons Act of Canada, effective January 1, 1952. Under the Blind Persons Act, however, while the allowance was continued at $40 per month, the means test was retained.
On behalf of the blind in the age group 21-69 the Canadian National Institute for the Blind are now seeking justice through the amendment of the Blind Persons Act of Canada to provide a basic federal government allowance of $40 per month, freed from the means test.
The registered blind of Canada were the first seriously handicapped group to be recognized as eligible for special government allowances, and for over 17 years their needs were met in association with the old age group. In fact, their extra living costs, compared to the aged, were recognized through a slightly higher ceiling for the means test.
The net effect of the 1951 legislation was to establish a disadvantageous differential for the blind of 21-69 years of age when compared to the general age group of 70 years and over, with whom they had been associated theretofore.
It is a well recognized fact that the extra living cost due to blindness is accentuated in proportion

to activity related to income earning effort. A blindness allowance free from the means test would provide a basic security and, therefore, would be a source of encouragement in taking fuller advantage of rehabilitation services leading to productivity and additional income.
I am sure hon. members on all sides of the house view this request of the blind in a sympathetic way. I sincerely hope the government will bring in the amendment that is requested by the blind association.
Four years ago, at the first opportunity I had to speak in this house, I suggested that it would be well to broadcast the opening of parliament so that the people throughout the length and breadth of this land, from one ocean to the other, would have the opportunity of hearing their parliament opened. We now have the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation television department. I am sure we will all agree that last Saturday, when the President of the United States was here, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation did an outstanding and admirable job of televising. From those who are able to receive the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation television programs, I understand that the corporation are doing an excellent job in that field. I now suggest again that the opening of parliament be broadcast and, if possible, that portions of it be televised. It might be better if it were completely televised rather than just broadcast.
During the election campaign previous to August 10 I had occasion to tour my riding of Hastings South many times. As many of you know, Hastings South produces the best cheese produced anywhere in the Dominion of Canada. Not only that, but very frequently more cheese is produced in the county of Hastings than in any other county in the Dominion of Canada. In Belleville we have the Ontario cheese marketing board. Cheese has been a commodity that has had its ups and downs, but I am pleased to have this opportunity, on behalf of the cheese producers of the county of Hastings, to thank the Liberal government and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) for the way in which they have treated the cheese producers.
You will recall, I am sure, that under the co-operative marketing act of 1939 cheese production was supported to the extent of 24 cents on the basis of legislation permitting 80 per cent of the average price over the last three years. You will recall, too, that last year was a provincial election year for Ontario, so they supported cheese production with an additional 6 cents, making a base price of 30 cents. You will also recall that this year the Ontario government saw fit, whether or not because it was an election

year in the federal field, to withdraw their support of 6 cents. However, in the words of one member of the marketing board which, as I said, has its headquarters in my home city, the federal government came to the assistance of the cheese producers in the way it has always done over the years.
The federal government bought 5,500,000 pounds of cheese of last year's make at 30 cents. It paid 30 cents for that cheese to take it off the market so it would not spoil the sale of this year's make. I am informed that the government has now sold at least half this cheese at between 32 and 35 cents a pound, and the profit that has been made on this deal will now be returned to the cheese producers in the province of Ontario.
Much has been said about the decline in prices. It so happens that in the dairy field the highest prices in the history of the country are being received for dairy products. Coming back to the cheese problem I may say, as I have said in my own constituency, that it is one which is entirely a problem for the province of Ontario. The maritimes do not produce anywhere near the amount that is consumed, so Ontario sells cheese in the maritimes. In Quebec they produce slightly less than the people eat, so there again is a small market for Ontario cheese. The western provinces of course produce very little cheese, and there is a fertile market for Ontario cheese. So I say thanks to the Minister of Agriculture on behalf of the cheese producers of my constituency for the way in which the government has helped them.
During the campaign I think we heard more frequently than anything else a discussion of the lack of housing accommodation. I am sure my constituency is no different from any other. Certainly we need houses. It would be well, I think, for us to review the housing situation and what has been accomplished. It might also be well to read that portion of the speech from the throne in which reference is made to housing. It reads as follows:
While more houses are being built this year than ever before, the growing population of Canada requires a continued expansion of housing. You will be asked to consider measures to increase and broaden the supply of mortgage money so that more people with moderate incomes will be able to find facilities to assist them to build their own homes.
In the field of housing the unprecedented rate of construction which has continued throughout this year may well mean the establishment of a new record level of building accomplishment in 1953. From the beginning of the year until the end of

The previous record set in the year 1950 was exceeded this year by about 2,250 completions.
During the same month new housing starts totalled 69,500 compared with 53,500 in 1952 and 61,700 in 1950. Another important factor tending to indicate a new completion record is that at the end of August 71,500 housing units were in various stages of construction as against a figure of 56,300 at August 31 of last year. Whether or not a new level of completions is reached this year will depend largely on the extent to which builders concentrate on the completion of these units rather than undertaking the construction of additional housing.
The increased production of new houses this year also reflects rising personal income accompanied by continued stability in building costs. Construction costs, which have spiralled to new levels with each post-war year, increased only slightly in the year ending last April despite the high level of construction. During that period the cost of house building, as measured by the combined index of residential building material prices and wage rates, showed a rise of only 2 per cent. Added impetus to increased house building has also been provided by an increased flow of institutional mortgage funds into the field of residential construction. In the first quarter of this year, mortgage lending for new residential construction in nonfarm areas was valued at $75-4 million and covered 11,500 dwellings. The figure represents a 38 per cent increase in amount and a 36 per cent rise in the number of dwellings over the totals for the first quarter of 1952.
The increase in institutional mortgage lending was particularly notable under the joint loan provisions of the National Housing Act, together with direct loans approved by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The joint lending operations of the lending institutions and the corporation under the act reached a total of 18,500 loans for 27,000 units, and an amount of approximately $200 million during the first eight months of this year. Comparative figures for the same period of 1952 are 16,300 loans for 23,200 units and an amount of $170 million.

Again, we had the section of the act covering rental insurance. One section enables Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to enter into a contract to guarantee an annual return on rentals for approved housing projects for a period up to 30 years. Another section provides for direct loans by lending institutions of up to 85 per cent of the lending value of rental housing projects, where such guarantee of rentals has been given by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
